docs.title: Starting and stopping
docs.text:
On TandemApp's own host chatd is the controller's (TANDEM_CHAT=own, proxy/appchat.py). A new TandemApp starts with Chat off (OPS-288): no chatd runs, and the Chat tab says "Chat is off" with a link to Settings, App, What runs here, where an admin switches it on (and off) with a plan and its confirm. Switched on, the controller starts chatd with <state dir>/chatd.env and watches it; with no sandbox runtime chat works without its sandbox tools, and the page and the health page say so. Switched off, chatd stops as a hand stop and every chat route answers 503 chat_off. The switch is kept in the controller's config database and wins over TANDEM_CHAT once used (install.md). The rest of this section is about an engine box.

chatd runs beside the engine, and on an engine box TandemNode, TandemApp's agent there, owns it (SRV-823). Since engine API 1.7 the engine has no chatd launcher: ops/start.sh, ops/watchdog.sh and bin/tandem never start or stop it, and the engine's QSE_CHATD is node (TandemNode runs chatd) or off (nothing does). install.sh --with-chat --app-wheel FILE writes QSE_CHATD=node and TandemNode's unit with --chat on.

TandemNode's watcher looks once a minute. When the engine answers /health and chatd does not, it starts chatd, at most 3 times an hour (one line each in its log), and never restarts the engine for it. It starts none in setup mode, on an engine-only box (QSE_MODE=engine, a new install's default, OPS-260), while a hold pauses the watchdog, or after a stop by hand until a start by hand. An engine that comes up in engine mode stops a running chatd once, and its Chat tab says the chat is off and how to turn it on, without asking a chat route. After an engine start TandemNode ran itself, it starts chatd at once. Under systemd a start runs in its own scope, so a restart of TandemNode, its update included, never ends a chat run.

tandem-node chat status            # who owns chatd, pid, URL, /health, the watcher's count
tandem-node chat start | stop | restart
tandem-node chat logs [n]          # <state dir>/logs/chatd.log

~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem chat start | stop | restart | status | logs runs tandem-node chat. tandem chat stop ends open runs as interrupted. The launcher is TandemApp's ops/chatd.sh (chatd/ops/chatd.sh inside an installed wheel), the script the engine's launchers ran before engine API 1.7: the same pid file (<data>/chatd.pid), data folder and port, so a TandemNode takes over a chatd an older install started. It runs chatd in the engine's environment, under the first of: CHATD_PY, serve.env's PY, the install's venv (~/TandemLLM/venv), ./venv, $VIRTUAL_ENV, python3 (said so, with a warning below 3.11); chatd needs only the standard library, and the venv's cryptography for the MCP servers' stored secrets. chatd and the engine read one secrets file, QSE_SECRETS (~/TandemLLM/state/secrets.env in an install), which ops/make-secrets.sh writes; with no key there chatd makes forward.key in its data folder, which the engine reads too. chatd's address is QSE_CHAT_URL (http://127.0.0.1:8016), its data folder QSE_CHAT_DATA, ~/.tandemllm/chat by default.

ops/chatd.service is a unit for chatd alone, for a box without TandemNode; with it set the engine's QSE_CHATD=off.

The sandbox is optional: without a container runtime the chat answers and uses the file tools; ops/sandbox/install.sh adds the rest.

On a machine where TandemNode runs chatd:

tandem-node chat status            # who owns chatd, pid, URL, the watcher's count
tandem-node chat start | stop | restart | logs

docs.title: When the Chat tab says the chat service is not running
docs.text:
The tab probes GET /v1/chat-app/capabilities and never falls back to an in-browser mock (VIS-179). Any other answer than the chat API's is a panel with the cause, the server's message, the command and Check again; it checks again by itself every 5 s, growing to 30 s, and turns live without a reload.

the tab says why on the box The chat service is not running. 502 chat_unavailable: chatd does not answer tandem chat start chatd is running but does not accept this server's key. 403 forbidden from chatd tandem chat restart && tandem restart This engine build has no Chat tab server. 404 run the installer again Cannot reach the engine server. no answer tandem status

A live tab that loses chatd shows one banner, "The chat service stopped", and recovers by itself. ?chat=mock (and the Vite dev server) loads the in-browser mock, with a "mock data" badge; it is for dashboard development only.

As many runs talk to the engine at once as it has lanes (its /health parallel.n; 8 until chatd has read it, SRV-707); QSE_CHAT_MAX_RUNS fixes the number instead. The others wait as queued. chatd's own /health says how many (runs). A run that waits for a permission prompt gives its slot back until the answer comes, and takes one again for its next call. A run on a cloud model takes no slot: its calls run at the provider, not on the box.

An engine without the forward. An engine server from an older build (or another engine altogether) has no /v1/chat-app route. bash ops/chatd.sh start --front 127.0.0.1:4180 also serves the built dashboard on :4180 from chatd's own process, forwarding /v1/chat-app/* to chatd and everything else to the engine (chatd/front.py). The front signs every caller in as the owner, so it binds to a loopback address only and refuses any other host. To reach the Chat tab from another device, run TandemApp.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text: The dashboard's one switch (the admin password, QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN). With none set, every chat route answers anyone on the trusted network and the tab shows no sign-in. With one set, every chat route needs the dashboard session cookie or the admin bearer token (or trusted-local); the probe (GET /v1/chat-app/capabilities) still answers and says signed_in: false, and the tab shows the setup guide's sign-in card. A write with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site is refused.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• ~/.tandemllm/chat/chat.sqlite3 (WAL, mode 600): conversations, the message tree, runs, the event log, the queue, attachments' metadata. Blobs under blobs/<sha[:2]>/<sha>.
  • A VACUUM INTO copy once a day in backups/, 7 kept. A deleted chat stays in the trash for 7 days; text deltas in the event log are dropped after 7 days (the messages keep their text).
  • chatd's log has ids, counts and times, never message text.

A deleted chat goes to the trash for 7 days, and its sandbox stops at once. POST /v1/chat-app/conversations/<id>/restore brings the chat back, and its sandbox starts again on its next tool call. When the 7 days end, or on DELETE /v1/chat-app/conversations/<id>?forever=1, chatd removes the container and the chat's folders under workspaces/, homes/, egress/ and snapshots/. At its start chatd also removes every container whose chat is gone or in the trash, and logs each one.

docs.title: The sandbox (phase 2)
docs.text:
Each chat's tools run in its own container, tandem-chat-<id> from the image tandem-sandbox:1 (build it once: bash ops/sandbox/build.sh). chatd speaks the Docker Engine API over a unix socket, QSE_SANDBOX_SOCKET (default /var/run/docker.sock); Podman serves the same API, and ops/sandbox/install.sh (root once) sets up rootless Podman under the user tandem-sbx with its nftables rules. Every container is locked down whatever the runtime: uid 1000, no capabilities, a read-only root, --network none, 1 GiB of memory, 4 CPUs, 512 pids, no GPU. Its internet goes through chatd's per-chat proxy, which refuses the LAN and this box (sandbox_network per chat: on or off).

A chat's tool call gets its sandbox: the sandbox has priority over what the engine holds idle. The engine keeps itself at its own floors (the KV pool's hard floor and the request admission's floor), so a sandbox only has to leave room for a prefill's workspace: 2.7 GiB measured for a 203,052-token prefill of the 27B EXL3 6.0 on the Spark, 3.5 GiB at the full window. A sandbox starts when MemAvailable minus its limit stays at 4 GiB or more. When it does not, chatd asks the engine for the difference (POST /v1/cache/release): the engine gives back its free allocator blocks, its caches, the small models and idle conversations (to the NVMe when the spill is on), never what a running request uses. A call waits for its sandbox at most 60 s; then it fails with the reason and the numbers, the model reads them as the tool's result and the chat shows them on the call. The guard asks the engine first and then stops the least recently used idle sandbox under 3 GiB, and kills them all under 2 GiB; an idle sandbox stops after 30 minutes. The files stay.

A process the kernel kills at the memory limit (the cgroup's oom_kill count; the cgroup is the one the container's first process is in, so Docker, Podman and containerd are read alike) fails its call with "out of memory (4 GiB sandbox limit)". The default was 1 GiB until 0.11.3; headless Chromium drawing a Three.js app in software (SwiftShader) went past it, so render_page and the verify phase failed on the apps they check. A container made under another limit takes the current one at its next start. render_page and the laya kit start Chromium with --disable-dev-shm-usage (a container's /dev/shm is 64 MB) and one renderer. The check browser has WebGL2 (SwiftShader) and no WebGPU, and render_page says so in each result: with --enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-vulkan=swiftshader --use-webgpu-adapter=swiftshader headless Chromium 155 gets an adapter that draws offscreen but presents nothing to a canvas, so a page's WebGPU path is not checked. What fits in 1 GiB, measured on the Spark (peak of the container's memory, page cache included): pip install of pillow, numpy, imageio-ffmpeg and piper-tts 549 MiB; npm i of typescript, eslint, @playwright/test, react and webpack 531 MiB; a Vite build 254 MiB; render_page of a 6,000-element page at 1280x800 503 MiB, at 2400x2400 442 MiB, a WebGL page at 1920x1080 422 MiB; piper text to speech, 55 s of audio, 366 MiB; 60 s of 1280x720 video drawn with PIL and encoded with libx264 415 MiB; the same at 1920x1080, preset medium, 1,010 MiB; pandas with 2 million rows and a matplotlib plot 391 MiB; g++ -O2, four files at once, 784 MiB. What does not: libx264 at 1920x1080 with preset slow and its default threads, 20 g++ at once, a 1.5 GB numpy array. The sandbox has 4 CPUs while nproc counts the whole box, so a tool that starts a thread per core (x264, make -j, xargs -P) takes more memory than it needs: with -threads 4 the 1080p slow encode peaks at 652 MiB. Knobs:

  • QSE_SANDBOX_MEM_GB (4): each sandbox's memory limit
  • QSE_SANDBOX_FLOOR_GB (4): MemAvailable a new sandbox must leave after its limit
  • QSE_SANDBOX_WAIT_S (60): the longest a call waits for its sandbox
  • QSE_SANDBOX_MAX_RUNNING (4) and QSE_SANDBOX_TOTAL_GB (the two multiplied, 16): how many run at once, and their limits' sum
  • QSE_SANDBOX_IMAGE (tandem-sandbox:1)

Set them in run/local.env (chatd reads serve.env and local.env), then tandem chat restart. Without a runtime, starting a sandbox answers 503 sandbox_unavailable, bash, render_page and the terminals are not offered, and the file tools work on the chat's workspace folder.

The unit tests (tests/test_chatd*.py, tests/test_chat_forward.py) never reach a container runtime: tests/chatd_util.py points QSE_SANDBOX_SOCKET at a path that does not exist, and a test that needs a sandbox installs a fake one. On the Spark, Docker and the sandbox image are there, and before this the tests found them: bash was offered, the tools' order changed and the capabilities said the sandbox was installed. Only tests/test_sandbox_box.py (with QSE_SANDBOX_BOX=1) uses the real runtime.

docs.title: Sandboxes as Kubernetes pods
docs.text:
With QSE_SANDBOX_BACKEND=kubernetes (the Helm chart's sandbox.mode: kubernetes, chatd in the controller's pod) each chat's sandbox is a pod in the release's namespace, made through the Kubernetes API with the controller's ServiceAccount (a Role: pods, pods/exec and pods/log in that namespace; no Secrets, no other namespace, no nodes). chatd/k8s.py has the whole design; in short:

  • The pod: the same image and lockdown (uid 1000, no capabilities, no privilege escalation, seccomp RuntimeDefault, a read-only root, no service-account token, no DNS), memory as request and limit (2 GiB on a host without the engine), 4 CPUs, no swap, an optional runtimeClass. With a user namespace (hostUsers: false, the chart's default) uid 1000 in the pod is not the node's uid 1000, and every exec runs under a 512-process limit that the kernel counts per pod. It runs on the controller's node and is owned by the controller's pod.
  • The files: /workspace and /home/agent are subPath mounts of the release's own volume, the same folders chatd reads and writes, with POSIX ACLs that give chatd's uid and the sandbox's uid both access. A ReadWriteOnce volume is one node's, so the sandboxes run on the controller's node.
  • The network: a NetworkPolicy lets a sandbox pod reach only chatd's egress proxy port (3128) on the controller's pod, and nothing reach the sandbox. The proxy is chatd's (chatd/egress.py, the same checks) on one TCP port; a connection's address names its sandbox, and any other address is refused. At start a probe pod with the sandbox's labels tries the controller's own port and the Kubernetes API: when either answers, the cluster does not enforce NetworkPolicy and chatd offers no sandbox at all, saying so.
  • Commands are execs over the API's WebSocket stream. A kill at the memory limit ends the whole pod (OOMKilled): the call says out of memory and the next call gets a new pod with the files. An eviction says so. A pod that stays Pending is reported as capacity and deleted after the wait.
  • QSE_SANDBOX_MAX_RUNNING and QSE_SANDBOX_TOTAL_GB count chatd's pods in the cluster. The scheduler holds the memory, so there is no MemAvailable floor here. Pods whose chat has no running sandbox are deleted at start and once a minute.
  • The image is built in the cluster and imported on each node (ops/sandbox/build-k8s.sh): nothing is pushed to a registry, and the pods never pull it.

tests/test_chatd_sandbox_k8s.py tests the backend against a fake API; tests/test_sandbox_k8s_box.py (with QSE_SANDBOX_K8S_BOX=1, in a throwaway release's controller) on a real cluster.

A deleted chat goes to the trash for 7 days, and its sandbox stops at once. POST /conversations/{id}/restore brings the chat back, and its sandbox starts again on its next tool call. When the 7 days end, or on DELETE /conversations/{id}?forever=1, chatd removes the container and the chat's folders under workspaces/, homes/, egress/ and snapshots/. When chatd starts, it removes every container whose chat is gone or in the trash, and logs each one.

MCP servers: stdio servers run inside the chat's sandbox, HTTP servers are called from chatd through the same egress rules; their secrets are sealed in the store and never come back in an answer.

chatd reads and writes the chat's workspace and the sandbox's home on the host (the file tools, the files pane, uploads, snapshots and undo, the Open WebUI runner's files), and the sandbox can change both at any moment. So no such access follows a symlink (chatd/workspace.py, SEC-1): it walks from the folder's root one directory at a time, each opened with O_NOFOLLOW from the one before, so a folder swapped for a symlink after a check cannot redirect it; a write goes to a new file (O_EXCL) in the verified folder and is renamed over the name; a read takes a regular file only (a FIFO would block chatd). A path with a symlink on the way is refused, and the file tools say so.

docs.title: The port preview
docs.text: The port preview shows an app that listens in the sandbox. Since 0.12.2 an app's answer goes on to the browser once its head is read, so an event stream or a long-poll shows as it arrives. A page, script or style sheet up to 8 MiB is read whole and rewritten; a bigger one passes as it is, with X-Tandem-Rewrite: skipped. The app has 300 s to start its answer. A browser that leaves ends the relay in the sandbox, and the idle stop can stop it again.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: An image goes to a model that reads images; a text file goes into the prompt, and its tokens show on its chip as soon as it is added (the composer uploads it then). When a message is sent, each of its attachments is saved in the chat's workspace under uploads/ (/workspace/uploads/<name>, a free name, cut to 255 bytes with its extension kept). When it cannot be saved there (uploads/ is a symlink, the disk is full), the message is sent all the same: the attachment keeps its stored copy and the prompt gets one line saying it is not in the workspace and why. The message's text files share a budget of a quarter of the window's free room, at most 32,000 tokens; a file past it is not inlined: the prompt gets one line with its name, size, tokens and path, and the chip marks it "as a file" before the send. A request that still does not fit names its cause: the attachment, its message and its tokens, or the largest part.

docs.title: Web search
docs.text:
web_search(query, max_results?) is a built-in tool. It answers a numbered list of results: title, URL, snippet, and date and engine when the provider gives them. The model cites the URLs and reads a page with web_fetch. The search runs in chatd on the host, not in the sandbox.

provider request setup duckduckgo (default) POST https://html.duckduckgo.com/html/ with q, kl (region), kp (safe search), df (time) none searxng GET <base>/search?format=json with categories=general, language, safesearch, time_range an instance URL with json in search.formats; an optional auth header off the tool is not offered
  • Egress: chatd/egress.py request() with a host list. DuckDuckGo reaches html.duckduckgo.com on public addresses only. SearXNG reaches the configured host and port only, a private address included. chatd refuses a redirect to another host.
  • Errors are tool results: DuckDuckGo's rate limit or bot check (HTTP 202), SearXNG's 403 (JSON format off), 401, 429 (limiter), a timeout, an unreachable instance, an answer that is not JSON. No results is not an error.
  • Settings (Chat settings, Web search): provider, searxng_url, searxng_auth_header and its value, max_results (1 to 20, default 8), safe_search (off, moderate, strict; default moderate), language (empty for any, or de, de-DE), time_range (empty, day, week, month, year), timeout_s (2 to 30, default 10). chatd seals the auth value with the secrets vault (proxy/secrets.py) and never answers it; answers carry searxng_auth_set.
  • A chat's web_search setting overrides provider, max_results, safe_search, language and time_range; null follows the global settings.
  • The tool's default policy is always: the user picks the provider in the settings. Set it to ask in the tools list for a prompt per search. The Now line reads Searching the web for "<query>".
  • A new chat gets web_search in its tools; an existing chat turns it on in the composer's tools menu.
  • OpenAI's web_search_options field stays refused by the API (docs/server.md): the engine has no search backend of its own.
GET  /v1/chat-app/web-search                 {settings, providers, safe_search, time_ranges, max_results_limit}
PUT  /v1/chat-app/web-search                 partial settings; searxng_auth_value null clears it
POST /v1/chat-app/web-search/test            {settings?, query?} -> {ok, provider, message, count, ms, results}
PATCH /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/settings  {web_search: {provider?, ...} | null}

docs.title: Permission modes
docs.text:
Each chat has a permission mode, and the chat settings hold the default that a new chat gets. A test run on a phone (2026-10-13) asked six times for bash commands such as grep and cp, which cost 20 s of tapping, and every one of them ran inside the chat's own sandbox. The three modes:

  • Ask: every risky call asks first, as before 0.8.2.
  • Auto, the default: a call that stays inside the chat's sandbox runs without asking. That covers bash, reading and writing files in /workspace, and render_page. A call that leaves the sandbox still asks: web_fetch to a domain this chat has not fetched before, an MCP tool that its server does not mark readOnlyHint, and an imported Open WebUI tool whose file imports a network or process module (requests, urllib, socket, subprocess and the like). rm or rmdir aimed at /, /workspace or a home directory asks too.
  • YOLO: nothing asks, and everything runs.

Some limits hold in every mode. A deny rule refuses the call, and so does a tool set to "never". A tool set to "ask" asks. Plan mode offers only the read tools. The sandbox stays locked down: no LAN, no host, and the internet only through chatd's proxy.

A call that runs without a prompt still leaves a record. Its tool card and tool.started carry approved: "auto" or "yolo" ("user" after a prompt, "rule" for a rule or an always policy), and the chat's event log gets a tool.auto_approved event with the call's one-line summary. The run's mode is on run.started, on the assistant message (permission_mode) and, after a change during the run, on run.mode. A change applies from the next call. The routes:

GET  /v1/chat-app/permissions/mode                       {default, modes}
PUT  /v1/chat-app/permissions/mode                       {default: ask|auto|yolo}
PATCH /v1/chat-app/defaults                              {permission_mode} -> the capabilities' defaults
GET  /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/permission-mode     {mode, effective, default}
PUT  /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/permission-mode     {mode: ask|auto|yolo}

A bash rule names a command's first word, or its first two for programs with subcommands (git push, npm install). A chained command (&&, ||, ;, |) runs without a prompt when every part has an allow rule, and is refused when any part hits a deny rule. "Always allow" on it saves a rule for each part not yet allowed. A command with $(...) or backticks matches no rule.

PATCH /conversations/{id}/settings takes permission_mode too. A chat from before 0.8.2 has none and runs in the default mode.

A bash rule names a command's first word, or its first two for programs with subcommands (git push, npm install); grep tilt saves grep. A chained command (&&, ||, ;, |) runs without a prompt when every part has an allow rule, and is refused when any part hits a deny rule. “Always allow” on such a command saves a rule for every part no rule covers yet, and the prompt names them: “Always allow cd, node, echo, cat”. Until 0.8.2 it offered only the first word, which never covered the whole command, so the prompt came back: one chat saved cd 11 times for cd /workspace && node ... > run.log 2>&1; echo "exit:$?"; cat run.log. Store schema 6 keeps one copy of each duplicate rule. A command with $(...) or backticks matches no rule and offers no “Always”. All of this matters in Ask mode; Auto runs bash in the sandbox without asking.

docs.title: Agents mode: a main agent with workers
docs.text:
A chat setting, agents, off by default (VIS-E15). With it on, the main agent talks with the user and plans, and gives every file write and every multi-step build or fix to a worker with the task tool. A long agent loop kept every file it wrote and read in its context: one chat on 2026-10-17 grew from 25k to 162k tokens in about 50 minutes, and its compactions read 131,505 tokens again each time. In Agents mode the file text lives in a worker's context and goes with it.

  • The main agent has read_file (at most 200 lines or 12,000 characters a call), glob, grep, web_search, web_fetch, render_page, present, the library, todo_write, task and the chat's MCP tools; no bash, write_file or edit_file. Each of its results is cut at 12,000 characters, and a repeated read of an unchanged workspace answers with the earlier call's id.
  • A task is {title, brief, expect}. The brief has four lines, Goal, Files, Constraints and Check, and no code: a code fence, more than 4 HTML tags, a run of more than 8 lines that look like code, a line of minified code or a "CODE:" block. A brief that breaks this is refused before any worker starts; its length is free. The brief describes the job and the worker writes the code: on 2026-10-17 a main agent wrote a whole clock page in its thinking and sent it in a 7,968-character brief, the worker copied it with a bug it had found, and the main context reached 64,240 tokens. A cap on the brief's length made the main agent cut requirements to pass, so there is none. If a brief still holds code, the worker treats it as a suggestion and fixes the bugs it finds.
  • The worker's message holds the task's number and title, the brief, expect, the todo list and then the user's message that started the run, word for word (an attachment by its name and path), so the brief scopes the job and need not repeat the request.
  • A worker is a full run on a hidden task conversation: a fresh context (the worker's instructions from packages/system/workers/, its tools, the brief, the todo list and the user's message), the chat's sandbox, /workspace, permission mode and rules, the parent's run slot, at most 40 model calls (task_max_steps), its own compaction and the verify phase. Its engine session is chat-<chat>-task-<n>; its memory notes are off. One worker at a time, at most 8 a run (task_max_per_run).
  • The worker ends with a report in a fixed shape. chatd parses it, sends it back once when a field is missing, builds one from the record when it is missing twice, and at the step cap makes one report-only call whose tool calls never run. Below the report chatd adds its own check: the files the snapshot diff says changed, the calls that ran, and the checks the report claims with no call behind them. The main agent reads at most 8,000 characters of it; the whole is in /workspace/.tandem/tasks/<n>/report.md.
  • Stop stops both. A message sent while a worker runs reaches the main agent after the report, and the worker as a note on its next tool result. An interrupted worker leaves its parent interrupted; Continue resumes the worker, then the parent, and never runs a cut-off write or command again.
GET   /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/tasks              {tasks: Task[]}
GET   /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/tasks/{task_id}    {task, messages, seq}
PATCH /v1/chat-app/conversations/{id}/settings           {agents} -> the settings + reread_tokens
PATCH /v1/chat-app/defaults                              {agents} -> the capabilities' defaults

The events and types are in dashboard/src/chat/CONTRACT.md, section "Tasks (VIS-E15)". With Agents off, every request is the one the single loop sends (tests/chatd_replay.py).

docs.title: Testing a Chat-tab bug
docs.text: A Chat-tab bug is tested on a recorded conversation, not with a new model run: tools/chat_trace.py replays a chat's snapshot through chatd with the fake engine in seconds and checks the requests it builds (--reread names every request that does not only append, --store puts the recorded screenshots back); tools/prefix_check.py sends those requests to a served engine one token each and reports what it read again; tools/chat_fork.py --at TURN:STEP replays up to a step and runs the live model from there for a few steps (--patch gives the call before it a fixed result). Each tool's usage text says the rest.

docs.title: Chat tab (beta): known limitations
docs.text:
The Chat tab is in beta in this release, and a Beta pill beside it says so. We know of these limits and have not fixed them yet:

  • The agent loop does not yet work the way Claude Code does (epic VIS-E10). Its prompts are not kept prefix-stable from step to step (SRV-375). Old tool results and old thinking stay in the context until a compaction (SRV-365). A compaction writes a general summary, not the task's state (SRV-373). Nothing notices when the model repeats the same failing approach with different calls (SRV-367). render_page passes on Chromium's console noise (SRV-369). Long tool output has no "see more" paging (SRV-371). Searches run in the main context, with no sub-agents (SRV-381).
  • The engine reads a short Flash-Next chat again on its next turn when the answer ended inside a verified block (ENG-235).
  • A request that arrives during a prewarm still waits 0.5 to 1 s (SRV-349).
  • When memory reaches its ceiling, the engine drops the parked chat without writing it to the NVMe, so its next turn starts cold.
  • Images only: there is no video input (VIS-97).
  • The 5.05 Flash-Next pack's full-pack load and generation are not yet verified.
  • Parallel decoding does not raise throughput over one request at a time: three requests together took 27.18 s against 27.03 s one after another, though the later ones start sooner.
  • The phone layout's keyboard behaviour is not verified in Safari on an iPhone.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: Importing Open WebUI tools and uploading a skill zip answer not_available (501). Uploads of attachments are phase 1's.

docs.title: The conductor
docs.text:
The conductor is the layer between a client and the weights. With it on, the server serves one model, TandemLLM: the weights with the conductor in front (server/conductor/). For every request it decides which profile applies, what kind of task the turn is, how long the model may think, and which hidden text goes into the prompt. While the model writes, it watches for loops, empty answers and broken tool calls, and acts at fixed points. It does not change the model's arithmetic: the tokens come from the same greedy decoding. Every decision, acted on or not, goes to one journal.

This page is the overview. Each section links to the full rules.

docs.title: Modes and headers
docs.text:
--conductor-config DIR (QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG in serve.env) switches the conductor on. Without it the server serves its own model name and none of this runs.

The box's mode decides whether ops/start.sh passes a directory (OPS-260). QSE_MODE=engine, a new install's default, starts the engine alone: no config directory, --conductor raw, no decision models, narrator, shadow reader or roles, and no chatd. QSE_MODE=chat (install.sh --with-chat, the Setup Guide's Chat (beta) switch, or run/local.env) starts the conductor with its directory, the small models the profile names and chatd. Left empty, a box whose conductor directory exists (it ran the conductor before the setting; a leading ~ counts as the server reads it) is a chat box, and any other box is engine only, so an upgrade keeps each box's mode; QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG=off set by hand stays engine only. install.sh and the Setup Guide always write the setting, so only a bare checkout with it empty goes by the directory: a tool that makes the default directory there (tools/library_install.py, tools/conductor_eval.py) turns that checkout into a chat box at its next start. The last block of ops/serve.env applies the mode after the profile, run/setup.env and run/local.env. /health and /v1/models say "mode": "engine" or "chat" and what is loaded (the conductor and its monitor's mode, the decision models, the narrator, the loaded roles, whether chatd answers). On an engine-only box there is no conductor: X-Tandem-Profile picks no profile, and every request runs on the raw path under the engine's own name. With it, /v1/models lists TandemLLM alone, and a request that names any other model, the engine's own name included, runs as a TandemLLM request.

mode what runs off no config directory: the engine alone, under its own name raw the release's path, byte for byte: no class, no note, no effort change, no monitor shadow every rule decides and writes to the journal; nothing acts on the profile's decisions act, and the monitor runs each task in its policy's mode

A request picks its profile with X-Tandem-Profile: <name>; an unknown name is a 400. X-Tandem: raw or shadow lowers the mode for one request. No header raises it. Every response carries X-Tandem (the mode it ran in) and X-Tandem-Profile (the profile). --conductor raw|shadow|on sets the session monitor's mode for the server, and a profile's mode caps it.

docs.title: Which profile a request gets
docs.text:
The conductor knows a client by its requests (headers, tool shapes, fixed system texts), never by a word list. A request resolves in this order:

  1. the X-Tandem-Profile header;
  2. the profile mapped to the client: opencode gets coding, Open WebUI and the dashboard's Playground chat, the Hermes agent hermes, the Chat tab (chatd, client kind chat-app) chat-app;
  3. tools, when no profile maps the client and the request offers a function tool with tool_choice other than none: an OpenAI SDK loop, curl, a benchmark (SRV-621; settings.tools_profile, empty turns the rule off);
  4. settings.default_profile, general on a new box.

The journal row says which rule picked it (extra.profile_source).

profile for what it turns on raw, bench locked nothing: the raw engine coding opencode every routing decision, packages, the loop guards, the tool-call checks, the claim check, status lines chat-app the Chat tab (beta) coding's policy without status lines in the answer hermes the Hermes agent coding's policy, with status lines in the reasoning chat Open WebUI, the Playground (beta) class-aware effort and packages, the reasoning guards, the same-call guard overnight unattended opencode runs, by header coding plus the session tasks, higher caps, a push when the client has gone tools API clients that offer tools the client's prompt, token for token; the loop guards and tool-call checks act general any other client class-aware effort and packages

The tools profile adds nothing to the prompt. It asks no class question: that side call made a full tool-eval-bench run take 1.23 times raw's time. Each act it takes is a journaled monitor event, so a request with no act gets the raw request's prompt.

docs.title: The router: one class per turn
docs.text:
Before a request queues, the router decides what kind of task the turn is. The shipped classes are code_edit, debug, design_ui, drawing, three_d, writing, plan, research, summarize and chat. Only a new user message asks a classifier. A turn that carries only tool results keeps the session's class, and so does the first message after a compaction.

flowchart TD
    req[request] --> prof["profile<br/>header, client, default"]
    prof --> side{"a side request's shape?"}
    side -- yes --> small["small plan<br/>no note, capped output"]
    side -- no --> new{"a new user message?"}
    new -- yes --> cls["Qwen classifies<br/>raw, thinking off, choice grammar"]
    new -- "no: a tool turn" --> keep["keep the session's class<br/>(first turn: the profile's default)"]
    cls -- "below 0.45" --> keep
    cls -- class --> plan["plan<br/>effort, cap, note, packages"]
    keep --> plan

The router's path from a request to a plan. A client's side request gets a small plan of its own. A tool turn keeps the session's class. A new user message asks Qwen; below 0.45 the turn keeps the session's class, or the profile's default class on a first turn.

In the shipped router the served model classifies its own requests: raw, thinking off, its answer limited to the class ids by a choice grammar. Every class's probability comes from the answer's first token. The answer counts at 0.45 or more. Below that, the turn keeps the session's class, or takes the profile's default class on a first turn. One exception covers a first turn whose top class builds something and leads the second by 0.1: the turn takes that class (SRV-255). On 216 labelled prompts the served model was right 0.949 of the time and a small decision model 0.782. The classifier reads the head and the tail of the new message. On TandemApp's controller, your own decision model can answer the decider stage's questions in place of the built-in one, per question, in shadow or A/B first (decision-providers.md).

No word list decides anything. The classifiers read a digest of the new user message, its head and its tail, sized to what each stage reads. Two more stages exist and are off by default in the router document: Qwen classifying inside the conversation the engine already holds (classifier.context_stage, for follow-ups and long prompts; every class is a single-letter token, so one forward's softmax is the answer), and a linear probe on Qwen's own hidden rows (classifier.probe_stage).

class what effort packages code_edit write, change, refactor or extend code xhigh coding (core), testing, Laya's test skills, test-web, test-cli, test-api, test-data, test-lib debug find and fix a bug, a failing test, an error, a crash xhigh the same design_ui the look of a page or an app high testing, Laya's, ui-design drawing draw, paint or animate with code high testing, Laya's, three drawing skills three_d a 3D scene or model high testing, Laya's, threejs-scene (core), photo-to-3d, voxel-seasons writing prose: an essay, an email, documentation medium none plan plan an approach before building high none research look up, compare, explain medium none summarize summarize given text, or a compaction off none chat small talk or a short question medium none

The router's shipped classes, with each class's effort and packages. A package marked core goes in on every turn of the class.

docs.title: Effort and the thinking cap
docs.text:
The class sets the turn's effort, and the engine enforces each level as a cap on the reasoning:

effort reasoning cap off thinking off low 1,024 tokens medium 8,192 high 16,384 xhigh none below the 32,768-token backstop (D2)

At the cap, the monitor closes the reasoning with the model's own closing phrase. The model reads the phrase; the client receives </think> and the answer. The engine turns thinking off in the prompt's tail, so nothing before the tail changes. A client's own number of reasoning tokens always wins, and so does its thinking off. An effort word such as reasoning_effort: medium is a ceiling on the router's level. The coding and overnight profiles ignore the word, because opencode sends medium on every turn.

docs.title: Packages and skills
docs.text:
The class's plan goes into the prompt as a note: the effort sentence, the class's rules, and packages. A package is a text that tells the model how a kind of work is done well: a task skill, a test skill, a card that lists the client's tools. A package marked general, and the class's core skill (threejs-scene for three_d), go in on every turn of the class. A second question picks one package among the rest, or none.

Packages fit the request's tools (SRV-243). A package that needs a shell or a file write stays out when the tools cannot do it, or gives way to its fallback. On a plain Open WebUI chat a landing page request used to get the testing packages, call tools the chat did not have, and take 518 s. A package whose result a client tool delivers (send, schedule, post) can stay out when the user wants it done (SRV-615); this ships in shadow.

The library holds 44 longer skills behind a BM25 index, with no embeddings. The model searches it from its own scripts (GET /v1/library/search?q=...), and the router can retrieve from it under a profile's library switch, in shadow in coding and hermes. packages.md lists the shipped packages and how each is measured.

docs.title: The note and its replay
docs.text:
The note goes into the last message, just before its end token. Every later turn of the session replays it at the same token position, so the resident prefix and every cache keep matching. The note is never streamed, never counted in usage, never stored in the suffix store, and a request with a note skips the response cache.

A later note carries only the parts no live note of the session already holds (QWEN38_NOTE_DEDUP, parts). Replayed notes have a budget of 16,000 tokens (injection.max_replay_tokens); over it the oldest note goes, and the turn reads everything after it again. Before the dedup, a turn in an Open WebUI agent chat read 35,442 tokens again (49 s) when the third full copy crossed the budget.

docs.title: Side requests
docs.text: opencode sends title and summary requests beside the session's turns, and the Hermes agent sends a title request. The router knows them by shape: no tools, and the client's fixed instruction at the head of the system message (structural.side_shapes). A side request asks no classifier, gets no note and changes nothing in the session. Thinking is off, and the output is capped at 64 tokens for a title and 256 for opencode's summary. A side request of at most 8,192 prompt tokens goes ahead of every waiting turn. Before this, the router classed one title request as code_edit at xhigh, the model wrote 5,567 tokens for it, and the session's real turn waited 54 s behind it.

docs.title: Compaction and sessions
docs.text:
opencode's compaction request is the class summarize: thinking off, no package, nothing replayed. The first user message after it (continue) keeps the session's class, and the class's note goes in again at the compacted history. The engine serves the compaction as a continuation of the conversation it already holds, so the prefill reads one turn instead of the whole history (caches.md).

A session is the client's conversation id (opencode's x-session-id, Open WebUI's X-OpenWebUI-Chat-Id). Without one it is a hash of the conversation's head, split further by each chat's first turn, so two chats that open with the same message stay apart (SRV-225). Before that split, a new agent chat started with 27 turns and 21,216 session tokens of earlier chats.

The notes give the model {tandem_url}: the request's own address plus /s/<token>, a random 12-character token kept 48 hours. Library reads and other calls from the model's scripts under that address are filed to their session in the journal.

docs.title: The session monitor and the loop guards
docs.text:
The router plans a turn before it runs. The monitor watches the turn while it runs and acts only at four safe points:

point when actions SP4 the prompt is rendered, before the prefill a hidden note at the tail, a thinking cap SP1 a verify block is committed close the reasoning, give up SP2 the end token is written, before the client sees it continue hidden, give up SP3 the answer ended and its tool calls are held repair a call, have the model write it again, give up

The shipped policy allows at most 2 acts a request and 6 a session hour, and never the same hidden action twice in a row on one turn. A give-up is one visible sentence with finish stop.

The tasks, by group:

  • Reasoning: D1 closes a reasoning block that repeats itself, and D2 closes any block at 32,768 tokens, or at the output limit less 2,048.
  • The end of a turn: E1 continues an empty answer, and sends tool calls the model wrote inside its reasoning as the answer when they parse. E2 checks a claim of done against the tool evidence since the last write.
  • Tool calls: C4 repairs a call that does not parse when the fix is not a guess. C3 asks for something different when the same call comes a third time after identical results. C5 has the model write two changing calls (send, schedule, create, write, delete) one at a time; it acts in tools only. C1 and C2 (risk floors, project rules) run in shadow.
  • Across turns: S1 (a checker gate stuck), S2 (state files not read after a compaction) and S4 (20 minutes without progress) act in overnight. S5 runs on every client and notes a problem stated three times, or a build turn with nothing written after three minutes.

The tool-argument loop guard stops a tool call whose arguments repeat. In one case the model wrote the same 97-character row of a tile map 12,866 times: 65,536 tokens over 327 s, and nothing was written. The guard now stops such a call within about 2,000 tokens of the loop's start. When the client sends the stopped call back, the history keeps its first 1,500 characters and one marker. After a repeat, loop escape (SRV-475) samples the next turn with the model card's settings until the session makes progress.

docs.title: The Chat tab's run monitor
docs.text:
chatd, the service behind the Chat tab (both in beta), runs its own agent loop and its own limits (chat.md). A run ends interrupted after 100 model calls, and the same call with the same arguments three times in a row ends it too. The stall rule (SRV-677, chatd/stall.py) catches a run that edits the wrong place. A check is a render_page call or a shell command the run has already run once. A check makes progress when its target is new, when its text changed (numbers are masked), or when its screenshot changed in kind (a 32 × 18 thumbnail, correlation under 0.3). The rule fires on a streak of at least 4 checks with no progress, at least max(12, 3 × the run's median gap) steps long, with at least 3 edits and 60 % of them on three files or fewer.

It acts twice. First, a note in the tool result tells the model to step back, list its hypotheses and test the cheapest one with a minimal repro. If the streak goes on as long again, a second note follows and the run ends interrupted; Continue goes on from there. The note rides in the tool result, so the prompt prefix stays the same. In the case behind it, a three.js page rendered near black, and 37 steps changed the lighting and the exposure in three files and rendered the page seven times. The cause was the materials' colours, and the same-call guard never fired because no call repeated.

docs.title: The journal and the dashboard
docs.text:
The router and the monitor write one journal: the table conductor_events in the usage ledger's file, kept 30 days. A request under the conductor writes one router row, and each monitor decision writes its own row. The journal stores each hidden text once, by its hash. GET /v1/conductor/sessions/{key}/export?format=md lists what the model saw that the client did not. Prometheus counts every decision and act (qse_conductor_*).

The configuration is a set of versioned JSON documents outside any repository: profiles, router, roles, packages, settings, and the monitor's policy. The dashboard's Conductor view shows the live decision feed and edits every document. The view checks a save and shows its diff; the save then becomes a new version with a note, and the next request uses it with no restart. A profile can also show the user what the conductor does, as short status lines in the reasoning or the content (ui.states).

docs.title: Raw mode for benchmarks
docs.text: X-Tandem: raw, or the locked profile raw or bench, serves the release's path byte for byte. The one difference is where a plain API client's reasoning goes: to reasoning_content (SRV-617). Benchmarks that measure the engine itself send this header. tools/row3.py --no-server refuses a server that lists TandemLLM. benchmarks.md says which settings a score must name.

docs.title: Measured effect
docs.text:
tool-eval-bench.md has every row; each row is one run, and run-to-run noise is about 2 points. On Qwen3.8-27B (EXL3 6.0, 2026-10-19, 69 scenarios):

row score time raw, xhigh 97 12.4 min conductor, tools 95 15.0 min bench-nopk: turn class and effort, no packages 96 13.5 min bench-pk: turn class and effort, with packages 94 26.0 min conductor, chat 91 28.0 min
  • Without packages the conductor scores the same as raw. Packages double the time and add no points on this model.
  • In hard mode (28 scenarios) tools scored 91 against 84 for raw. On the 0.12.2 build the next day, raw and the conductor without a profile header both scored 86, and tools 82 twice. Which part of the conductor makes the difference is not tested.
  • On Ornith-1.5-122B (0.13.0, 2026-10-21), tools scored 96 against 93 for raw xhigh, and the conductor 84 against 80 in hard mode. There bench-pk scored 97 against 94 for bench-nopk, in 20.1 min against 14.1. One run each; this needs a second run before it says anything about packages.

docs.title: Where to read more
docs.text: topic page profiles, the router, classes, packages in the plan, side requests, compaction, sessions chat-mode.md a client's own thinking budget and effort word server.md status lines shown to the user chat-mode.md the package library and its search chat-mode.md, packages.md session addresses server.md the session monitor, safe points, policy chat-mode.md tool-call checks, the claim check, the loop guard, session tasks chat-mode.md, the claim check, the loop guard, session tasks the journal and metrics chat-mode.md, tandemapp/METRICS.md compaction as a continuation caches.md the Chat tab and chatd (beta) chat.md memory notes memory.md the dashboard's Conductor view dashboard.md the /v1/conductor/* API contracts/conductor-v1 benchmarks, raw and conductor benchmarks.md, tool-eval-bench.md the session monitor, every task session-monitor.md status lines, the voice, the shadow reader status-lines.md the conductor in front of another backend proxy.md

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The engine serves its own web page at /dashboard/. It answers the question a log cannot answer at a glance: what is the engine doing right now, for whom, and how fast. All of it is about 45 KB of gzip for the parts every tab loads, and the box needs no Node to serve it.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
view what it shows Chat the Chat tab: a chat whose runs live on the server (chat.md) Performance the Live panel on top, then time to first token, tokens per round and acceptance over the last 5 minutes, then speed history from the usage ledger. The Recent requests chart plots decode tok/s against prompt length; a replay (the response cache, a summary written ahead) decoded nothing and is never a point there, nor in any average, percentile or live rate, and the switch lists the replays with their TTFT. Side-lane requests (0.3.27-test) are not plotted either. The y axis ends at twice the 95th percentile of the points, and a point above it is a triangle at the top edge with its value in the tooltip. The Parallel page shows every request in flight on every backend, one row each in the Lanes panel (Lanes) Usage a year of tokens as a heatmap, with totals for today, 7 days, 30 days and the year, split into input, cached input, output and reasoning Dev the live server log, filterable, with a detail view for each request; Export saves the whole log as a text file (Log export) Playground a streaming chat against the engine's own API, with tools, parameters and the figures of each answer Conductor how TandemLLM decides, and every knob of it: the live decision feed, the task classes and their policy, the classifier stages and thresholds, the session monitor's journal and rules (the tool checks' floors, project rules and reminders, the reasoning arms, the empty-turn nudges, the session tasks S1, S2 and S4 with their texts, patterns and push) and what the session tasks hold per session right now, profiles and roles (each role's contract: kind, window, preemptible, latency budget, fallback, writes, the tokenizer hash and the forms of sharing it allows), the Packages screen (G2: one list of every package, task skill, test skill, card and library skill with its kind, source, switch, general flag, the tokens of the text that goes in on the engine's tokenizer against its limit, the classes that list it and its injections, shadow notes and library picks in the last 24 h and 7 d; a search that asks the library's own index and filters by kind, class, switch and over the limit; a package's detail with its text rendered or raw, frontmatter, reference, classes, recent rows and a library skill's BM25 neighbours; inline packages edited in a Markdown editor with the token counter and the limit, a file on the box read-only or copied to an inline package; attach and detach on the router's classes, general packages first; every save checked first with its diff shown, then a new version with a note, and the versions with restore; the Library tab: each profile's retrieval switch beside the picks its shadow journaled), session timelines with the export of every hidden text, the Memory screen (the session transcripts kept on the box, a keep switch, the Markdown and JSON export, the transcript settings; a session's turn snapshots counted in its line and named in each block's runtime section with the turn's outcome (J1); the Disk cache tab: what the disk tier holds against its budget, the NVMe's free space, the hit rate, the most-hit prefixes with a preview for opencode heads and packages only, its events, its settings -- on or off, the budget in GB, the time to live, admission, the free space it keeps, at least 50 GB -- and a clear button; the admin token is asked for to read them), precision and promotion, and the eval reports: the classifier's, and the suite report of tools/tandem_eval.py with its verdict, n and the indicative label, both arms per suite. Every edit is a new config version; writes ask for the admin token when the page has no session (chat-mode.md) Backends the proxy's registry (docs/proxy.md): each backend's health, models, requests in flight and cost today; add one after a test connection, edit, delete; the key field is write-only and shows the key's last 4 characters; a field a TANDEM_* variable sets is locked and names it; the models with their public ids, output limits (empty: the provider's list, else none), prices (USD per million tokens, the list prices of the release one click away) and per-model switches; the background memory writer's switches on the form (mode auto, off, shadow or on, the spend cap a day with a no-cap box, runs a day, the prompt cap; a field a variable sets is locked), and on the backend's page the day's runs and spend, each model's resolved mode and why, and in shadow where the would-be blocks go; the ordered routing rules; the users and their keys, each shown once. With no backend it opens on Setup. On an engine without --backends it says how to turn the proxy on. Relayed requests appear in Usage (a backend and a user filter, the cost of priced models), in Dev and in Performance with a backend tag, "measured at the proxy", and "not reported by this backend" where the proxy sees nothing System the engine's settings and the box's state (memory, GPU, caches), with 30 minutes of history kept in the browser; below them the hosts: this machine with the engine's process and every backend on it, and each remote backend's machine, down to the GPU memory of its processes (docs/proxy.md) Health what is wrong, in words, and what to do about it: one sentence at the top, then a card for this TandemApp, each engine host, the plugins and the pairing codes refused lately. A card shows its checks in the order they ran, its findings worst first with the fix, and a button where TandemApp can fix it itself (Start, Rotate the token, Upgrade, Restart chatd) or can show the steps. A changed host key shows both fingerprints and how to pair again, and nothing that connects (proxy.md) Setup the Setup Guide, which picks a model and installs it; a box in setup mode opens on it (setup.md)

The System view shows the machine behind each backend, down to the GPU memory of its processes, through a collector on the same machine or a small one on the backend's own (proxy.md).

The engine card carries one neutral line, the speed check: “passed for 0.4.0 · ” when the build has a speed guard report (the release ships its own, release/speed-guard.json), “not run for this build” otherwise; the numbers are in its tooltip and on the Conductor's Compare screen. It is no warning: the speed guard is the release process's check, not something to act on in the dashboard.

docs.title: The views at a glance
docs.text:
view what it reads for Chat /v1/chat-app/* chatd's chats, runs and sandbox (chat.md) Usage /v1/dashboard/summary, /usage a year of tokens, cost by backend and user Performance /v1/dashboard/live (SSE), /requests, /metrics, /parallel the Live panel, the history, the lanes, every request at once (monitoring.md) Dev /v1/dashboard/logs, /logs/export the live log, filterable, and each request's detail: its timings, cache source, tokens, the conductor's decisions and why it ended; a memory-gate refusal is an error line with the allocated and reserved figures Playground /v1/chat/completions the OpenAI API itself Conductor /v1/conductor/* decisions, documents, sessions, memory (conductor.md) Backends /v1/config/* backends, models, prices, rules (backends.md) System /v1/dashboard/system settings, the memory plan, the hosts Setup /v1/setup/* the engine's Setup Guide: models, weights, the install job

The nine views, in the order of the navigation rail. Chat sends messages and Setup installs a model; the other views only read, except where an edit makes a new version of a document or a configuration row.

The Live panel reads as an instrument: (1) the state line, in the server's own words, and the panel's report on its own stream; (2) the two big figures with 5-minute sparklines, each leaving the request's warm-up out and reading a dash when nothing runs; (3) tokens a round and milliseconds a round, the two factors of the engine's speed; (4) one lane per request in flight: state, client, profile, tokens split into thinking and content, time to first token, and a strip with one segment per state; (5) the newest status line, and what the agent did between two turns; (6) how each of the last 20 requests ended, in one sentence; a row opens its detail in the Dev view.

The Performance view, Engine page: the Live panel with a request writing, the decode and prefill rates, and the last requests. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Usage view: a year of tokens, requests and cost, filtered by model, client, backend and user. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Dev view: the live log, which never holds prompt or answer text, and the recent requests. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Playground before the first message: the chat on the left, the system prompt and the sampling parameters on the right, the engine's own figures for each turn below. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Conductor view, Overview: decisions and the session monitor's acts over 24 hours, the classifier's latency, the roles online and the task classes. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Conductor view, Sessions: each session's client, profile, current class, turns and the hidden notes it carries. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Conductor view, Memory, the Notes tab: the live notes by scope, with kind, status, writer and use. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The Backends view with a vLLM, an SGLang and a DeepSeek backend, and the line for this engine's own settings. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

The System view: the engine, the memory, the GPU, the queue, the caches and the machine. Demo data from the dashboard's mock server (npm run preview:mock), not a measurement.

docs.title: Live activity
docs.text:
Recorded on the served engine; requests outside the demo session are blurred.

The Live panel streams GET /v1/dashboard/live over server-sent events. While a request runs it gets four events a second, otherwise one.

A line at the top says what the engine is doing now, in the server's own words:

  • Prefilling 36,864 of 48,210 (76 %), with the prefill rate and an estimate of the time left;
  • Thinking or Writing, with the decode rate and the tokens so far;
  • Calling tool write_file, with the size of the arguments written so far;
  • Waiting for client: running tool bash, between two turns of an agent;
  • Idle or Draining.

When the client's socket closes while the engine still works for it, the line says so in red: "client disconnected 12 s ago".

Under the two big figures (decode and prefill tok/s, each with a 5-minute sparkline) the panel shows tokens per round and milliseconds per round over the last second. Each request in flight gets a row: its state, its client, tokens split into thinking and content, time to first token, the rates, and a timeline strip with one segment per state. When an agent sends its next turn, the row says which request it continues and what the client did in between ("continues chatcmpl-7f3a after 8.4 s, client ran bash").

A list of the last 20 requests says how each one ended, in one sentence: "abandoned by the client after 73 s of silent prefill, 0 tokens sent". Abandoned, failed, timed-out and cancelled requests get a red mark. Refused and rejected ones get an amber mark. A row opens the request's detail in the Dev view.

It also reports on its own stream, "streaming · 4/s", "no update for 3.0 s" or "reconnecting since 4 s". A silent page is never mistaken for an idle engine.

docs.title: Lanes
docs.text: The Parallel page of Performance (#/performance?tab=parallel) ends with the Lanes panel: one row per request in flight, on the engine and on every backend, kept in its place until a few seconds after the request ends. A row names the backend and the model, the engine's slot, the client and the session, the state, the tokens with the thinking part apart, the decode rate now and on average, the time to first token, the prefill rate, the cache hit, the cost so far and the time since it arrived. Its numbers come from GET /v1/dashboard/parallel (proxy.md).

docs.title: Held for memory
docs.text:
A request that waits for memory before its prefill (parallel-requests.md) is shown as held, never as a hang. The server writes three lines for it (server/api/activity.py memory_lines), and the page shows them as they come:

  • what the turn needs and why it waits: "This turn needs about GiB to read new tokens; GiB is free, other turns and the caches hold of it, and must stay free for the system". When the check of its pages holds it, the line says "for its pages" and "while it reads" (0.15.4);
  • what happens meanwhile: chats with a higher priority ahead in the line, another chat's turn that is reading and its time left, idle cache being given back, or the time it has waited so far;
  • how the wait ends: the chat continues by itself as soon as memory frees, Stop cancels it, and it gives up only after 3 h without memory, with the time left.

    • On the Engine page, when the request the Now line follows is held, the line reads "Waiting for memory" with the three lines in place of a rate. The request's card lists them, and in the table, which cards replace below 1,100 px of width, they are the state cell's tooltip. In the Lanes panel the state says that the request waits for memory and continues by itself, its tooltip holds the three lines, the TTFT cell counts the wait, and the prefill cell stays empty. activity.memory in the live view carries the same figures as numbers.

docs.title: Where the words come from
docs.text:
Every state and every sentence comes from the server (server/api/activity.py), and the page only formats numbers. Our loop keeps the state it needs anyway, and a sampler reads it once per tick: no statement runs per token for the dashboard's sake. With the activity on and a stream open, the release gate found the text byte-identical and the round time unchanged within noise. --live-activity off turns the activity fields off; the counters and rates stay.

A tick costs 410 to 470 µs of CPU at 4 Hz. Each tick is encoded once and sends it to every open stream, and it allows at most 4 streams.

docs.title: Log export (0.15.4, SRV-803)
docs.text:
The Export button is the last one in the Dev view's Log toolbar. It saves the whole log as one text file, to attach to a bug report. The file holds every line the server keeps (the newest 10,000, at all levels), whatever level and search the page shows. It starts with a header: the version, the commit, the uptime, the time of export in UTC, the line count, the time of the first and the last line, whether older lines have already left the ring, and whether --log-content is on (contract/dashboard-v1/logs-export.example.txt). Each line reads <UTC time> <level> <message>, as the copy button writes it, and a traceback stays one entry.

The file comes from GET /v1/dashboard/logs/export, under the same access rule as the log itself. The server names it tandemllm-<version>-<time>.log, takes one snapshot of the ring without the engine lock or a stream place, and leaves the ring as it was. The export adds the header and nothing else, so the file follows the log's own rule: the engine writes no prompt or answer text into its log, and it withholds an exception message that quotes the request, unless --log-content is on. The standalone proxy answers the same route from its own log with commit: unknown and log content: unknown, because it has no such flag and does not vouch for its lines.

After a save the panel shows "Saved as" with the file name and an "Open the file" link to the route, for a browser that kept no file. The next press clears that line. A browser that cannot save a file the page builds is told so and gets the same link. A server that sends no file within 60 s shows as an error, and the button can be pressed again. On a phone the toolbar wraps, so the button stays in view.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
contracts/dashboard-v1/ holds a JSON Schema for every JSON response of /v1/dashboard/* and a valid example of each. Both sides test against it. The backend's tests validate real responses from the server. The dashboard's tests validate the examples and every response of its mock server (npm run test:contract in dashboard/). A change to a field bumps contract_version, and the contract's README lists every change. The live and session endpoints are at version 1.1.

endpoint what GET /v1/dashboard/live requests in flight, the engine's state, the last 20 stops, 5 minutes of history GET /v1/dashboard/summary totals for today, 7 days, 30 days and the year GET /v1/dashboard/usage tokens and speed per day or hour, with filters by model and client GET /v1/dashboard/requests finished requests, newest first GET /v1/dashboard/system settings, memory, caches, ledger and disk GET /v1/dashboard/logs the server log, as JSON or as a stream GET /v1/dashboard/logs/export the whole log ring as one text file with a build header (plain text, no schema) GET /v1/dashboard/parallel every request in flight on the engine and every backend, for the Parallel page: one lane each (lanes), the ones just finished (recent), each backend's figures (backends), the sums (totals), one decode sample a second per backend (series) and the engine's slots (engine_slots); ?since=<unix s> sends only the newer samples. The engine and the standalone proxy both answer it (schema, example) GET /v1/dashboard/metrics the /metrics page, for the Performance view's 5-minute figures GET /v1/dashboard/session whether an admin password is set (password_set), whether the login is on, and the session's expiry POST /v1/dashboard/session a session cookie for the admin token (only with a password set and the login on; the page has no sign-in screen yet)

docs.title: No password
docs.text:
The dashboard asks for no password anywhere: no sign-in screen, no sign-out button, no token dialog. Open http://<host>:8000/dashboard/ and every view works, the Conductor's editors and the Memory screen (notes, transcripts, the disk tier) included. You can read and edit them straight away.

This holds while no admin password is set on the server, which is the default (server.md). Then anyone who can reach the port can read and change everything the dashboard shows:

  • per-request counts and timings from the usage ledger: tokens, speeds, cache hits, finish reasons, the kind of client and a short hash of its API key;
  • what runs now: each request's state, its client, the names of the tools it calls (not their arguments), and the last 20 stops;
  • the server log. No line carries prompt or answer text, unless the server runs with --log-content, which lets exception messages quote a request;
  • the engine's settings: its command line and every QWEN38_* and QSE_* variable, with the home directory written as ~. Variables named like a token, key, secret or password show <redacted>;
  • memory, GPU, cache and disk state, and the Prometheus counters of /metrics;
  • the conductor's documents, the memory notes and the session transcripts, which it can also edit, archive and delete.

Keep the server on a trusted network. Never put it behind a reverse proxy that faces the internet while no password is set.

docs.title: With a password set
docs.text:
Setting QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN in secrets.env and restarting turns the admin rule back on for every admin route. The dashboard has no sign-in for that yet: with the login off its read-only views keep working, while edits and the Memory screen show the server's 401 as an error, and a banner says a password is set. Unset the token and restart to open the dashboard again. API clients send the token as Authorization: Bearer <token>.

TandemLLM's own calls to itself (the router's question to the engine, client_kind internal, 0.3.43-test, VIS-60) are left out of Usage, the summary, the request counter, the model and client filters and Dev's Recent requests; the "show internal" switch on Usage and on Recent requests lists them, each with the request it served (parent_request). In the Live panel the cached share is never above the client's prompt (VIS-58): the prompt is what the client sent, and the notes TandemLLM added show as their own figure (15,957 cached · +4,625 hidden).

docs.title: While the engine restarts
docs.text: A browser that opened the dashboard before keeps working through a restart without the proxy's help (OPS-131): its service worker (dashboard/pwa/sw.js) answers a page load that gets 502, 503 or 504, or no answer, with the cached shell. The page then asks the worker (./sw-away), says the engine is restarting, polls /health every 3 s and reloads when it answers. API calls (/v1/) never go through the worker. A first visit has no worker yet and gets the proxy's answer. The engine's status responder answers the proxy's fallback for the page meanwhile (the engine's operations.md).

docs.title: Usage ledger
docs.text: server/api/ledger.py writes one SQLite row per request: the model, the kind of client (curl, an OpenAI SDK, opencode, the dashboard), token counts, timings, draft acceptance and the finish reason. It never stores prompt or answer text. Usage and Performance read it through the dashboard API. --usage-ledger PATH turns it on, and --usage-retention-days bounds it (at least a year plus a margin, so the Usage view has its year). A benchmark server started without the flag writes nothing.

docs.title: Building and testing
docs.text:
The app is written in TypeScript with Lit components and built by Vite. Its charts are hand-drawn SVG, and it loads nothing from a CDN. The built page, dashboard/dist/, is a build output and not in git; the server serves it from there. The dashboard-dist workflow (.github/workflows/dashboard-dist.yml) builds it on every pull request and push to main with npm ci and the lockfile, runs vitest and the size budget on the result, checks that a second build gives the same bundle hash, and hands the page to the jobs that package it. python3 tools/dashboard_bundle.py build does the same build on your machine and writes dist/bundle.json, the bundle's hash; docs/proxy.md ("The built page") has the fetch of a released bundle and how the server names the bundle it serves.

cd dashboard
npm ci
npm run dev:mock        # the app against a mock engine, token "mock" (?mock=nologin: the login off)
npm test                # unit, contract and build tests
npm run build           # type-check and build dist/ (not in git)
npx playwright test     # end-to-end, Chromium and WebKit, desktop and phone

A mock engine can play scenarios for the Live panel (an agent turn with a chunked prefill and a tool call, a client that leaves during a prefill, one request per stop reason) and failure modes (expired session, server errors, dropped streams). Those end-to-end suites also run against server/app.py --fake-engine, which serves the real API with a scripted engine and no GPU. dashboard/README.md has the developer details.

docs.title: Decision providers
docs.text: The conductor makes small decisions all the time: which kind of work a message is, which package fits it, whether the user asked to remember something, whether a tool's output shows a failure. Each is a typed question with a fixed set of answers, and a small decision model answers it in tens of milliseconds. A decision provider is who answers. The built-in one is the conductor's own decider; you can put your own model in its place, per question, behind an API of yours.

docs.title: What a decision is
docs.text:
A question has an id, its wording, its options ({id: what it means}) and the text it is about (a digest of the user's message, the session, or a tool's output). The answer is one option id with a probability. The conductor asks its stages in order (the cascade): the decider stage first, then the served model's own stage where the router document has it. A stage's answer is taken when its probability reaches the stage's threshold (0.8 for the decider by default); otherwise the next stage is asked, and with none left the turn falls back to the router's default.

A provider answers in the decider stage's place. Which stages a question asks is the router document's choice: to have a provider answer the class question, the decider stage must be enabled there.

question id asked by answers classify the router, on a new user message the router's classes packages the router and the library the package names, and none deliverable the router what the turn is to deliver memory_intent the memory notes yes / no: does the message ask to remember, forget or recall memory_gate the memory writer yes / no: anything worth a note in the session judge the tester's questions after a turn failure / clean / unclear, ok / failed / incomplete

docs.title: Where the questions are asked
docs.text:
Two conductors exist, and a provider serves one of them:

  • The controller's conductor (TandemApp's own, switched on from the page) runs around requests relayed to backends: the harness asks it before a request goes out, its judge after the turn, its memory writer in the idle time. Every question above is asked in the controller's process, and a provider can answer all of them today. Its decider role names self by default, which on a controller answers nothing: without a provider the decider stage there says decider_no_endpoint and the served model's stage decides.
  • The engine's conductor (inside a TandemLLM engine, through the engine extension) asks the engine's own decision models in process, in the engine's idle window. Its questions decide what goes into the prompt, so they touch the engine's tokens. Providers do not serve it in this version. Routing them needs one of: the extension asking the controller (POST a question to the controller, one LAN hop of a few milliseconds, inside the idle window, with the controller's answer or the built-in on any failure), or the engine reaching the provider itself (the provider set pushed to the engine with its keys sealed for that host). Either changes the engine's decisions and needs the GPU check (G3) in a stop window first.

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text:
kind what answers configured with builtin the conductor's own decider (its decider role's endpoint; tester for the judge) at a model per question models per question systemone-http any service that speaks the systemone wire below endpoint, API key, model and timeout, each also per question hook a decision.ask hook of hooks: an adapter you write for any other API shape the hook's id plugin a running plugin's provider (plugins): decision/ask over its stdio target: <plugin>/<provider>

A running plugin's providers are also there on their own, in shadow, as <plugin>/<provider>: asked off the request's path and journaled, never used. A provider of kind plugin naming the same target takes its place, with your mode.

docs.title: The systemone wire
docs.text:
Three calls, the shapes pinned in contracts/engine-api-v1/decision/systemone.schema.json. With an API key every call carries Authorization: Bearer <key>.

POST {endpoint}/v1/systemone:

{"state": "Rename the variable cnt to count in utils.py and run the tests.",
 "model": "auto",
 "questions": {"q": {"type": "choice",
                     "instructions": "What kind of work does this request ask for?",
                     "criteria": {"code_edit": "change code in a project",
                                  "chat": "a question or a conversation"}}}}

answers

{"contract_version": "1.0", "model": "my-decider",
 "answers": {"q": {"type": "choice", "choice": "code_edit",
                   "probabilities": {"code_edit": 0.93, "chat": 0.07}, "confidence": 0.93}},
 "usage": {"input_tokens": 16, "output_tokens": 0},
 "routing": {"model": "my-decider", "reason": "default"},
 "path": "single", "latency_ms": 21.4}

GET {endpoint}/readyz answers {"status": "ready", ...} when it can serve. GET {endpoint}/v1/models lists the models with their limits (context_tokens, question_tokens, max_options): the conductor sizes the text it sends to what the model reads, at 3.5 characters a token (512 and 192 tokens when not given). model is the one the provider maps for the question, auto by default.

tools/systemone_example.py is a whole provider in the standard library: run it, point a provider at it, then replace its decide() with your model.

python tools/systemone_example.py --port 8720 --key "$MY_KEY"

docs.title: Setting one up
docs.text:
The API is /v1/fleet/decision-providers (the configuration's rights, as backends and hooks). A provider that answers the class question with its own endpoint and key, and the memory gate at the default endpoint:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/fleet/decision-providers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "My decider", "kind": "systemone-http",
  "endpoint": "http://decider.example:8720", "api_key": "<key>",
  "timeout_ms": 400, "mode": "shadow",
  "questions": {
    "classify": {"endpoint": "http://classes.example:8720", "api_key": "<another key>",
                 "model": "classes-v2"},
    "memory_gate": {}}}'
  • questions maps each question it answers; a question may set its own endpoint, api_key, model and timeout_ms, and takes the provider's for the rest.
  • A key is write-only: a string sets it, null clears it, and every answer shows only whether it is set, its last 4 characters and a sha256 prefix. Keys are stored sealed under the master key, never logged, journaled or exported; a controller move carries them inside its sealed handover and the new controller seals them again under its own master key.
  • The provider's own key goes only to its own endpoint's origin: a question with an endpoint on another host gets its own key or none.
  • One enabled provider may answer a question on or ab; any number may watch it in shadow.
  • POST .../{id}/test asks it once with a sample question; GET .../{id}/health probes it; GET .../report has the numbers below. The list (GET /v1/fleet/decision-providers) carries each provider's health from its last probes and probes nothing: an endpoint not probed since the provider last changed shows no probe, and the status unknown.
