  • A refusal is {error: {type, code, message, field?}} (contracts/conductor-v1 error.schema.json); field names the value it is about.

A provider's switches and keys are also keys of the settings interface's hooks scope (providers.<id>.<field>, settings). There a change is planned, versioned and can be restored with the other settings. Its keys stay write-only there; a change set that adds a question may set that question's key (providers.<id>.questions.<question>.api_key) in the same change.

docs.title: The Decision providers pages
docs.text:
Settings, Hooks, Decision providers shows who answers each question and who watches in shadow, each provider with its health and mode, and the report with its arms side by side: on, shadow and both sides of an A/B. A provider's page has each endpoint's probe and breaker, the mapping per question with the last four characters of its key, a test call, the fallback reasons counted from its recent calls, and those calls. Add a provider offers the three kinds, and a new one starts in shadow.

The mode, the A/B share, the sticky key, the questions and the keys are staged and go through the settings' review. The name, endpoint, model and time limit are written at once.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• on: the provider answers its questions. On any failure the built-in answer is used.
  • shadow: the conductor decides as without the provider. The same question goes to the provider beside it, off the request's path, and the journal keeps its answer, its time and whether it agrees with the conductor's decision. Nothing it says is used. Start here.
  • ab: a share of sessions (ab_percent, 0 to 100) get the provider as in on, the rest the built-in. The split is sticky: by session (default), user or request, the next one taken when the first is missing, and a provider's id seeds it, so two providers split the sessions differently. The router's class cache keeps each arm's answers apart.

docs.title: Health and fallbacks
docs.text:
A provider is not used for a call, and the built-in answer is, when:

reason what happened timeout no answer within its timeout (at most the stage's, 400 ms for the router's questions) unreachable, http_<code> the endpoint did not answer, or answered an error (http_401: the key) unknown_label the answer is not one of the options breaker_open five failures in a row, or a p95 at its timeout over the last minute: skipped for 30 s, then one probe call provider_down its last health probe (/readyz, kept 10 s) failed hook_off, no_answer, out_of_scope a hook provider's hook is off or in shadow, answered no decision, or its scope does not take the request replay_miss replaying recorded answers, and none recorded for this question not_granted the endpoint's host is not in the provider's grant, or is outside the LAN without its confirm (below)

docs.title: Where the text goes
docs.text:
A systemone-http provider is sent the question's text, a digest of what people wrote, so it takes the rules of a hook at the full payload (hooks). Making one, or changing where it or one of its questions answers, is a grant: it takes pairing's rights (403 trust_required without them; with no admin password set, only the controller's own machine). The grant (grant in the provider's view) names each destination host and whether it is on the LAN, who granted it and when. A host outside the LAN asks a second time: the write answers 409 confirm_needed with a confirm, and the same write with it grants it and records who confirmed. A call to a host the grant does not hold is not made (not_granted). In the settings interface a change of providers.<id>.questions that adds such a host is planned the same way (grant_keys, confirm_grant).

The stage's row in the conductor's journal names the provider (provider: {id, mode, arm?, fallback?}) whenever one answered or fell back; without a provider the row is as it was. The health view (GET .../{id}/health) gives each endpoint's probe, its breaker and its questions, and a status: ok, failing (a breaker not closed, or the last call within a minute failed), down (a probe failed) or off; in the list's view also unknown (an endpoint not probed yet).

docs.title: The journal and the report
docs.text:
Every provider call, and every decision of an A/B arm a, is a row of the conductor's journal (kind: provider, the question id as its task): the provider, its mode and arm, which answer was used, the provider's answer (label, probabilities, model, time, error), the built-in decision, agreement, the fallback's reason, and a hash of the question's text. The text itself is never in the row.

GET /v1/fleet/decision-providers/report?hours=24 reads them back per provider, question and bucket (on, shadow, ab_a, ab_b): calls, answered, failures, fallbacks and each fallback's reason counted (fallback_reasons, the reasons below), agreement in % (shadow), p50 and p95 of the provider's time (the built-in decider's in arm a) and the answers given.

Replay. tools/decision_replay.py --ledger <the usage ledger's file> > answers.json collects the recorded answers by their hash; a controller started with TANDEM_DECISION_REPLAY=answers.json answers every provider question from it, with no call, so a run replayed decides the same every time.

docs.title: A hook as the adapter
docs.text:
When your model's API has another shape, write a webhook for the decision.ask stage with the role decider (hooks.md has the signing), then a provider of kind hook that names it. The hook gets the question (its payload level decides whether the text comes too):

{"question": {"id": "classify", "type": "choice",
              "instructions": "What kind of work does this request ask for?",
              "options": {"code_edit": "change code in a project", "chat": "a question"},
              "model": "auto", "deadline_ms": 400, "state_chars": 63},
 "content": {"state": "Rename the variable cnt to count in utils.py and run the tests."}}

and answers with an option id, or with its probability:

{"action": "decide", "decision": {"answer": {"choice": "code_edit", "confidence": 0.91}}}

A bare id ({"answer": "code_edit"}) counts as sure (1.0). Keep the hook's own mode on: the provider's mode decides shadow and A/B.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text: With no provider (none stored, only disabled ones, or only ones for other questions), every decision of the conductor and every relayed byte is what it was; a provider in shadow changes no decision either (tests/test_decision_providers.py, tests/test_decision_providers_api.py). The same check with the engine's real models and tokens (G3) needs a GPU stop window; providers do not reach the engine's conductor in this version.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
TandemApp's terms. The engine's (anchor, round, StairCut and the rest) are in TandemEngine's glossary.

  • adapter The proxy's code for one backend kind: how it relays a route, where it reads cached and reasoning tokens, how it switches thinking. proxy/adapters/.
  • backend An engine or a cloud API behind the proxy: another TandemEngine, vLLM, SGLang, any OpenAI-compatible or Messages API server, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek. Each has a kind, a URL, models, an optional key, and switches (backends.md).
  • feature group One switchable part of the harness in front of a backend: class, effort, packages, side, loops, e1, tools, compaction, states, memory.
  • host collector The code that reads a machine's memory, CPU, GPUs, disks and the process behind each backend's port; tandem-app hostcollect on a remote machine.
  • L1, L2 The two layers of engine figures behind the proxy: L1 is the engine's /metrics page, L2 the plugin's per-request numbers.
  • preset A provider the Add backend form offers (OpenAI, OpenRouter, Z.ai, Ollama and the rest): its base URL for each protocol, its kind and how it takes a key. proxy/presets.py.
  • protocol What a backend or a client speaks: openai (chat completions, completions, embeddings, Responses) or anthropic (the Messages API).
  • plugin A small package inside vLLM or SGLang that posts each request's own times to the proxy.
  • proxy The router of requests by model id to backends, with one ledger and one dashboard: tandem-app, the controller (until engine API 1.8 also the engine's server with --backends).

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
A hook is your code at a point of a request's way through TandemApp: when it arrives, when the backend is chosen, just before it goes to the engine, on each streamed event, on the answer, on an error, after the ledger row. Add as many as you like at each point; they run in an order you set, and each one can watch, change, refuse or decide, as its stage allows.

The contract is contracts/hooks-v1: the stages, the call and result schemas, examples and a fake receiver. This page explains it and shows how to write a webhook.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Stage. Where the hook runs (table below).
  • Role. What it does there:
  • a transform changes the value with a patch;
  • a guard may refuse the request;
  • a decider chooses (a backend, a fallback, one retry);
  • an observer only watches.
  • Kind. How it is called: http (a webhook TandemApp POSTs to, signed), builtin (code shipped in TandemApp: set, deny, route, fallback, noop) or plugin (a running plugin's hook, target <plugin>/<hook>: plugins). mcp and inproc are reserved; until they exist a hook of those kinds is refused.
  • Priority. An integer; low runs first, ties go by id.
  • Mode. off, shadow (it runs and its answer is journaled, nothing is applied) or on.
  • Scope. Which requests it sees: model globs, backends, profiles, users, sessions, client kinds. Empty means all.
  • Failure policy. open (a hook that fails is skipped) or closed (the request is refused). Guards are closed unless you say otherwise.
  • Payload level. How much of the request the hook sees: meta (default), redacted or full.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
stage when may budget on failure called now request.received after auth, before routing modify, deny 150 ms open yes route.select choose backend, model, profile decide 150 ms open (the table's route) yes request.before_engine the final body before sending modify, deny 250 ms open yes decision.ask a question for a decision provider decide 400 ms open (the built-in answer) with decision providers stream.chunk each event of a stream observe async drop yes tool_call.detected the answer holds a call modify, deny 500 ms open yes tool.before_exec, tool.after_exec Chat, around a tool deny, modify 500 ms closed for guards with Chat's stages response.after_engine the whole answer modify, deny, one retry 1 s open yes request.error an upstream error before any byte went out choose a fallback 250 ms open yes request.finished the ledger row is written observe async drop yes memory.write a note about to be stored modify, deny 500 ms open with the memory writer session.start, session.compact session events observe, modify 250 ms open with Chat's stages engine.lifecycle start, stop, mode, settings applied observe async drop with engine control

stages.json has the fields a patch may touch at each stage. A field that holds what people wrote or the model answered (messages, prompt, input, tools, the answer's choices, the tool calls) can be changed only by a hook with payload full.

On a streamed answer, tool_call.detected and response.after_engine run after the stream has ended and only watch: the client already has the answer.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Transforms run first and chain: each sees what the ones before it made.
  • Guards run next, on the transformed value, and the first deny wins. The client gets 403 hook_denied with the guard's reason and an X-Tandem-Hook header naming it.
  • Deciders run after the guards; the first decide wins.
  • Observers see the final value, off the request's path.
  • A stage's budget is shared by its hooks per request. All sync hooks before the first token share 800 ms: when that runs out, the hooks left are not called and their policy applies.
  • No retries on the request's path; an observer is called once more if it fails.
  • Circuit breaker, per hook: five failures in a row, or a p95 call time at its timeout over the last minute (20 calls at least), open it for 30 s. Meanwhile it is skipped and its policy applies; then one probe call closes it again or keeps it open.
  • A closed hook that fails refuses the request with 503 hook_unavailable.
  • With no hook enabled, TandemApp relays every request byte for byte as it did without hooks.

docs.title: Writing a webhook
docs.text:
TandemApp POSTs one JSON document per call (call.schema.json):

{"hooks": "1.1", "id": "hd-...", "hook": "temperature-cap", "stage": "request.before_engine",
 "ts": 1763200000.0, "payload": "meta", "mode": "on",
 "request": {"request_id": "chatcmpl-px-...", "endpoint": "chat", "model": "example-model",
             "upstream_model": "example-model", "backend": "local", "profile": null,
             "user": "owner", "session": "s-1", "client_kind": "unknown", "stream": false,
             "protocol": {"inbound": "openai", "upstream": "openai"}},
 "event": {"sizes": {"body_bytes": 412, "messages": 2, "tools": 1,
                     "chars": {"system": 15, "user": 30, "assistant": 0, "tool": 0}},
           "params": {"temperature": 0.9, "max_tokens": 256}, "params_set": [],
           "tool_names": ["search"],
           "route": {"backend": "local", "model": "example-model", "attempt": 0}}}

request.protocol (version 1.1) names the client's protocol and the backend's: openai or messages (the Messages API). A hook always sees the chat shape. When both are messages the request passes through as the client sent it: a patch of a parameter with a Messages API field still applies, a patch of the messages, the tools or the answer does not (journaled refused, protocol_native; the hook's failure policy applies). Calls from version 1.0 had no protocol; contracts/hooks-v1/compat/1.0/ keeps them.

and reads the answer (result.schema.json):

{"action": "modify", "patch": {"temperature": 0.3}, "reason": "capped", "labels": {"team": "a"}}

continue (or an empty 200, or 204) changes nothing. deny refuses with your reason. decide carries a decision: {backend, model, profile} at route.select, {fallback: {backend, model}} at request.error, {retry: true} at response.after_engine, {answer} at decision.ask (a question of the conductor, asked through a hook decision provider). labels travel to request.finished. Any other answer, a status other than 200 or 204, or no answer within the timeout counts as a failure.

docs.title: Checking the signature
docs.text:
Every call carries X-Tandem-Timestamp and X-Tandem-Signature: v1=<hex>, the HMAC-SHA256 of <timestamp>. followed by the body's bytes, keyed with the hook's secret (the hks_... string TandemApp showed once when you made the hook). Check it on the raw bytes before you parse them, refuse a timestamp more than five minutes away, and refuse a delivery id you have already seen. While a rotated secret is in its grace, the header holds two v1= values: accept either.

Python:

import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import time

WINDOW_S = 300
seen = {}   # delivery id -> when; a shared store when the receiver runs more than one process


def verify(secret: str, headers, body: bytes) -> bool:
    """True for a call this TandemApp signed that was not seen before."""
    ts = headers.get("X-Tandem-Timestamp") or ""
    sig = headers.get("X-Tandem-Signature") or ""
    if not ts.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > WINDOW_S:
        return False
    want = hmac.new(secret.encode(), ts.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not any(hmac.compare_digest(want, part.strip()[3:])
               for part in sig.split(",") if part.strip().startswith("v1=")):
        return False
    delivery = json.loads(body)["id"]
    now = time.time()
    for k in [k for k, t in seen.items() if now - t > WINDOW_S]:
        del seen[k]
    if delivery in seen:
        return False
    seen[delivery] = now
    return True

A whole receiver with the standard library, capping the temperature at request.before_engine:

import json
import os
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

SECRET = os.environ["HOOK_SECRET"]


class Hook(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0))
        if not verify(SECRET, self.headers, body):
            self.send_response(401)
            self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
            self.end_headers()
            return
        call = json.loads(body)
        t = call["event"].get("params", {}).get("temperature")
        answer = {"action": "continue"}
        if isinstance(t, (int, float)) and t > 0.5:
            answer = {"action": "modify", "patch": {"temperature": 0.5}, "reason": "capped"}
        out = json.dumps(answer).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(out)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(out)


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 9300), Hook).serve_forever()

Node (the raw body, before any JSON parser):

const crypto = require("crypto");

const WINDOW_S = 300;
const seen = new Map(); // delivery id -> when

function verify(secret, headers, body /* Buffer */) {
  const ts = headers["x-tandem-timestamp"] || "";
  const sig = headers["x-tandem-signature"] || "";
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(ts) || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) > WINDOW_S) return false;
  const want = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(ts + ".").update(body).digest();
  const ok = sig.split(",").map((s) => s.trim()).filter((s) => s.startsWith("v1="))
    .some((s) => {
      const got = Buffer.from(s.slice(3), "hex");
      return got.length === want.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(got, want);
    });
  if (!ok) return false;
  const id = JSON.parse(body.toString("utf8")).id;
  const now = Date.now() / 1000;
  for (const [k, t] of seen) if (now - t > WINDOW_S) seen.delete(k);
  if (seen.has(id)) return false;
  seen.set(id, now);
  return true;
}

module.exports = { verify };

To try a hook without writing one, run the fake receiver: python contracts/hooks-v1/fake_server.py --port 9300 --secret hks_... --set temperature=0.3.

docs.title: Adding a hook
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/fleet/hooks -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "temperature cap", "kind": "http", "endpoint": "http://hooks.lan:9300/",
  "role": "transform", "stages": ["request.before_engine"], "priority": 10,
  "scope": {"models": ["qwen*"]}}'

The answer holds the hook and, once, its secret. Then:

  • POST /v1/fleet/hooks/{id}/test {"stage": "request.before_engine"} calls it once with the stage's sample event and shows the event it sent, what it answered and what it would change. Nothing is applied or counted. GET /v1/fleet/hooks/stages serves every stage's sample event (samples) beside the stage table.
  • PUT /v1/fleet/hooks/{id}/mode {"mode": "shadow"} lets it see real traffic without changing it; GET /v1/fleet/hooks/{id}/calls shows each call's outcome and, for a shadow, the diff (field names and sizes).
  • GET /v1/fleet/hooks/calls?request=<id> traces one request: every call the journals hold for it, across hooks and stages, in the order the request met them, each with its hook's name.
  • POST /v1/fleet/hooks/{id}/disable, /enable, PATCH, DELETE.
  • POST /v1/fleet/hooks/{id}/secret {"grace_s": 3600} rotates the secret; the old one keeps signing beside it for the grace.

The routes need the admin's rights. Granting full, moving a full hook to another endpoint and rotating a secret need pairing's rights (with no admin password set: from the controller's own machine).

A hook's switches (enabled, mode, priority, scope, policy, timeout and payload level) are also keys of the settings interface's hooks scope (hooks.<id>.<field>, settings). There a change is planned, versioned and can be restored with the other settings. The full payload keeps the same rules there: pairing's rights, and a second confirm (confirm_grant) for a destination outside the LAN.

A builtin hook names its target and options, for example a guard that refuses one model for one user:

{"name": "no big model for guests", "kind": "builtin", "target": "deny", "role": "guard",
 "stages": ["request.received"], "scope": {"models": ["big-*"], "users": ["guest*"]},
 "options": {"reason": "ask the admin for this model"}}

docs.title: The Hooks pages
docs.text:
The dashboard has all of this under Settings, Hooks.

  • Pipeline. The 15 stages as stops, in the order a request passes them, with the hooks at each stop in the order they run. Each row shows the mode, the kind, the scope, the priority, the failure policy and the breaker. Arrows and dragging change the order within a role. A move sets priorities, and a hook has one priority, so it moves at every stage it runs at. A bar shows how much of the 800 ms before the first token the hooks on the path use: each one's p95, added up.
  • Add a hook. Five steps: the stage, the role and the kind with its URL or built-in, the scope, the failure policy with the time limit, and the payload level. A new hook starts in shadow. A webhook's secret shows once, with the code that checks a signature.
  • A hook's page. Its state, breaker, figures and recent calls; a shadow call lists the fields it would have changed and their sizes. The secret's rotation is here, and the playground: one test call with the stage's sample event, and what the answer would do to a request.
  • Trace. One request by its id across every stage, read from the hooks' journals.

The switches (on, mode, order, scope, policy, time limit, payload level) are staged and go through the settings' review, so each change is planned, versioned and audited. Adding and removing a hook, its stages, its endpoint and its secret are written at once.

Replay is not built: the journal keeps no bodies. The Trace page says so and links the playground.

docs.title: Payload levels
docs.text:
level the hook sees meta (default) ids, the model, sizes, counts, timings, the scalar parameters, tool names. No prompt or answer text redacted meta and content, with keys, tokens and passwords replaced by [redacted:<kind>] (the conductor's redaction). If the redaction fails, the hook is not called and its policy applies full meta and content as they are

full is granted per hook, and the grant keeps who granted it and when. If the endpoint is outside the LAN (not loopback, a private or tailnet address, or a .lan, .local, .home.arpa or .internal name), the request answers 409 confirm_needed with a confirm token; send the same request again with "confirm": "<token>" to grant it. Changing a full hook's endpoint to another place outside the LAN asks again. A hook granted for the LAN checks on every call that the address it connected to is still on the LAN, and sends nothing otherwise.

docs.title: Shadow mode
docs.text: A hook in shadow runs on every request in its scope, off the request's path, on a copy of the value it would have seen. Its answer and what it would have changed are journaled; nothing reaches the request. Use it to try a new guard on real traffic before switching it on.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: GET /v1/fleet/hooks carries each hook's calls, failures, timeouts, p50 and p95 and its breaker. The controller's /metrics page has qse_hook_calls_total, qse_hook_failures_total, qse_hook_timeouts_total, qse_hook_latency_ms{quantile} and qse_hook_breaker{state}, labelled by hook id.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Hooks run in the controller. A hook that needs token ids or the decode loop runs inside the engine through its extension interface instead.
  • The journal of calls is kept in memory, the last 500 calls per hook.
  • A hook's answer is at most 1 MiB. A hook's timeout is at most its stage's budget; an async observer's defaults to 5 s, at most 30 s.
  • On a stream, hooks watch; they cannot change what was already sent.
  • request.error runs for failures that can still go elsewhere (a refused connection, 429, 502, 503); a backend that stays silent past its first-byte timeout answers 504 as before.

docs.title: TandemApp on Kubernetes with Helm
docs.text:
The chart charts/tandemapp runs TandemApp's controller in one pod. No image is built: every container runs a stock Python image pinned by digest, and an init container unpacks a release archive into the pod's volume and makes a virtualenv there from the archive's own wheels. The values are listed in the chart's README; the overview, the first page and backups are in install.md.

The procedure below is the one tested end to end (OPS-292) on a single-node cluster: Kubernetes 1.35 (MicroK8s, amd64) with Calico, the hostpath storage class on ext4, the nginx ingress controller behind a reverse proxy that ends TLS, Chat with sandbox pods, and an MCP bridge sidecar.

docs.title: 1. What the cluster needs
docs.text:
what why Kubernetes 1.27 or newer; 1.33 or newer with containerd 2 for sandbox pods sandbox.kubernetes.hostUsers: false (a user namespace per sandbox pod) needs 1.33 a storage class with ReadWriteOnce volumes, or a host folder (persistence.hostPath.path) one volume holds the state, the releases and chat's data a file system on that volume that takes POSIX ACLs (ext4, XFS) sandbox pods only: chatd and the sandbox are different users on the same folders an ingress controller (ingress.className) the page and the API; or reach the Service another way a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium) sandbox pods only: without it chatd offers no sandbox kubectl and Helm 3.12 or newer where you run the steps

The nodes pull the stock Python image (image.*). Nothing else is pulled at run time: the release comes on the volume, and the sandbox image is built in the cluster.

docs.title: 2. The release archive
docs.text:
The pod runs tandemapp-<id>.tar.gz: one folder <id>/ (the commit's first 12 characters) with the release's files (tools/app_release.py: no tests, no page sources), the built page in dashboard/dist, a wheelhouse/ for the image's Python and the nodes' architecture, and a RELEASE file (commit, page hash, date). The init container refuses an archive without <id>/proxy.

Build it on a Linux build host, from a fresh copy of the commit, so the archive depends on the commit and the pinned inputs only:

COMMIT=$(git rev-parse <tag or branch>)
mkdir build-1 && git archive "$COMMIT" | tar -x -C build-1
cd build-1
# Node 24.11.1 (check its tarball against nodejs.org's SHASUMS256.txt) on PATH
python3 tools/dashboard_bundle.py build --commit "$COMMIT" --prune-modules
python3 tools/dashboard_bundle.py verify
cd ..
WHEELS=$PWD/wheels bash <checkout>/charts/tandemapp/scripts/make-archive.sh \
    "$COMMIT" build-1/dashboard/dist out-1

WHEELS is a folder that holds exactly the wheels for the image's Python (3.12) and the nodes' platform: cryptography, psutil and their dependencies (cffi, pycparser, typing_extensions). Fetch them once with pip download --only-binary=:all: --python-version 3.12 --platform manylinux_2_28_x86_64 -d wheels cryptography psutil (arm64 nodes: manylinux_2_28_aarch64) and keep that folder; without WHEELS the script fetches the newest ones. make-archive.sh prints release.id and the archive's sha256.

Every entry has the commit's time and owner 0, and the entries are sorted, so the same commit, page and wheels give the same bytes. Build a second time from a second fresh copy (build-2, out-2) and compare the two sha256: they must be equal. Copy trees between a Mac and the build host with COPYFILE_DISABLE=1 tar --no-xattrs: a Mac's tar otherwise adds ._ files, which the packer refuses.

docs.title: 3. Before helm install
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace tandemapp

Sign-in with accounts (auth.mode: accounts, the only mode). User accounts with roles, sessions and API tokens are the sign-in; the admin-token mode of older charts (legacy) is gone and refused. The chart puts no auth secret into the pod's environment:

  • The Secret is mounted into the controller as a file (TANDEM_SETUP_CODE_FILE) that holds a one-time setup code. Leave auth.existingSecret empty and the chart makes it with a 20-character code; or name your own with auth.bootstrap.existingSecret (and .secretKey). Read it once:

    kubectl -n tandemapp get secret tandemapp-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-token}' | base64 -d; echo

Open the page, enter the code with the first owner's name and password. The code is single use and spent after 5 wrong tries. With no Secret at all (auth.create: false) each start logs a fresh code while no owner exists. - On a new install, make no admin token. A Secret named by auth.existingSecret (or the one an older chart made with an admin token) is the old admin token as well: a value of 32 characters or more there becomes an API token for scripts for 30 days once the owner exists (auth.md). Let the chart make the code, or give your own in a Secret named by auth.bootstrap.existingSecret, which is only ever a setup code. - Nobody signs in before the owner exists: every route but /health and the page shell answers 401. That includes kubectl port-forward, which reaches the pod on its own loopback: on Kubernetes (TANDEM_DEPLOY=kubernetes, which the chart sets) loopback is never trusted. - A new code, and a lost password, through kubectl exec (helm install prints both lines):

  kubectl -n tandemapp exec deploy/tandemapp -c controller -- env PYTHONPATH=/var/lib/tandemapp/current \
    /var/lib/tandemapp/current/venv/bin/python -m proxy users setup-code --config-db /var/lib/tandemapp/state/config.sqlite3
  kubectl -n tandemapp exec deploy/tandemapp -c controller -- env PYTHONPATH=/var/lib/tandemapp/current \
    /var/lib/tandemapp/current/venv/bin/python -m proxy users reset-password NAME --config-db /var/lib/tandemapp/state/config.sqlite3

reset-password prints a one-time code, valid 24 hours: sign in with it as the password, then set one. - Once the owner exists the health page asks to delete the Secret (bootstrap_secret_left). The mount is optional, so the pod starts without it; set auth.create: false (or auth.bootstrap.create: false) so an upgrade does not make it again. - A chatd on another host (chat.mode: external) needs a key of its own: tokens chatd-key FILE through the same kubectl exec, then give that chatd the key as QSE_CHAT_ENGINE_KEY.

Extra CAs. When the controller calls services with a private CA (engines over https, MCP servers), give it the CA: --set-file trust.extraCA=ca.pem.

docs.title: 4. Install
docs.text:
A minimal values file, values.yaml:

release:
  id: "0123456789ab"                 # make-archive.sh's release.id
  archive:
    url: ""                          # or an https URL the pod can fetch
    sha256: "<the archive's sha256>"
persistence:
  storageClass: <your class>
  size: 20Gi
auth:
  existingSecret: tandemapp-admin
  create: false
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: tandemapp.example.com
networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  ingressNamespaces: [ingress-nginx] # the ingress controller's namespace

helm install tandemapp charts/tandemapp -n tandemapp -f values.yaml

This is a bare TandemApp: the gateway only, Chat and the conductor off, no MCP bridge (OPS-288). Switch parts on from the page (Settings → App → What runs here) or with the values in section 6.

Putting the archive on the volume. Either:

  • release.archive.url and .sha256: the init container fetches it and checks the sha256; or

  • url empty: the pod waits in its init container release (up to waitSeconds, then it fails and retries), and helm install prints the line that copies it in:

    POD=$(kubectl -n tandemapp get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=tandemapp,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') kubectl -n tandemapp cp tandemapp-.tar.gz $POD:/var/lib/tandemapp/incoming/tandemapp-.tar.gz -c release

    The init container waits until the file's size holds still, checks the sha256 when it is set, unpacks the release to releases/<id>, makes its venv offline from the wheelhouse and points current at it. A release that is unpacked already is used as it is.

    Then:

    kubectl -n tandemapp rollout status deploy/tandemapp
helm test tandemapp -n tandemapp       # /health and the page through the Service

    and open https://tandemapp.example.com/: the setup wizard (pairing an engine host: install.md).

docs.title: 5. Ingress, TLS and a reverse proxy in front
docs.text:
• The Ingress sends everything to the controller except ingress.blockedPaths (/chat-engine, chatd's way to the gateway inside the pod), which go to a Service with no endpoints (503). Check it after the install: /chat-engine/health must answer 503 from outside.
  • A reverse proxy in front that forwards only some paths must still send the controller every prefix it owns: the list is in install.md.
  • TLS at the ingress: ingress.tls with a Secret for the host. TLS at a reverse proxy in front: leave ingress.tls empty, have the proxy forward plain HTTP to the ingress with the original Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For, and let the ingress controller trust them (ingress-nginx: use-forwarded-headers: "true"). The session cookie is marked Secure from X-Forwarded-Proto: https.
  • The chart's annotations turn buffering off and allow an hour per request: answers stream, and a long one takes minutes. A proxy in front needs the same.
  • Behind an ingress every client reaches the controller from the ingress pod's address, so the sign-in limit (5 wrong passwords a minute) is shared by all clients until auth.trustedProxy names that address (below).
  • The API paths. The ingress routes the OpenAI-compatible routes (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/responses, /v1/cache) and the Messages API (/v1/messages) by default, on a new install and an upgrade alike. /v1/models is always routed: the page reads it. ingress.api.openai: false or ingress.api.anthropic: false sends that protocol's paths to the Service with no endpoints (503). The page's Playground, its model windows and the developer view post to /v1/chat/completions, so ingress.api.openai: false breaks them through the ingress. Who may call is the controller's rule, the page's API exposure switch (accounts mode): while a protocol is "this machine", an API token from another device gets 403 api_not_exposed; "network" lets a token with the protocol's scope in. A signed-in page session always reaches the routes its role allows, whatever the switch says. On Kubernetes no caller counts as this machine, so a client with a token needs its protocol at "network". The chart tells the controller what it routes (TANDEM_INGRESS_API), and the health page says when a switch is on for a path the ingress blocks (exposure_unreachable).
  • The trusted proxy. With TLS ended at the ingress, set auth.trustedProxy to the ingress controller (TANDEM_TRUSTED_PROXY: a comma list of addresses and CIDR ranges, IPv4 and IPv6). Only then do its X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Real-IP count; without it every API token through the ingress is taken as sent over plain HTTP (exposure_plain_http) and every client shares one sign-in limit. An ingress controller's pod gets a new address when it restarts, so name the cluster's pod range rather than one address, for example with --set auth.trustedProxy=192.0.2.0/24\,2001:db8:42::/64 (write your cluster's own pod CIDR). An entry that is neither an address nor a range is ignored, and the health page names the variable (trusted_proxy_invalid).
  • networkPolicy.enabled admits the controller's port from ingressNamespaces and this release's pods only (extraFrom adds more). The kubelet's probes still pass.

docs.title: 6. Values that matter
docs.text:
The full table is the chart's README. The ones to decide:

value default what release.id, release.archive.url, .sha256 required, empty, empty the release the pod runs persistence.storageClass, .size, .existingClaim, .hostPath.path the cluster's default, 20Gi the volume; kept on uninstall (persistence.keep) auth.mode accounts the only value; legacy is refused (section 3) auth.existingSecret, .secretKey a Secret the chart makes the setup code, or an older release's admin token auth.bootstrap.existingSecret, .secretKey, .create empty: the Secret above the setup code's own Secret auth.trustedProxy empty the ingress controller's address or its pods' CIDR range when it ends TLS (section 5) ingress.api.openai, .anthropic empty: routed false blocks that API's paths (section 5) chat.mode empty: off on a new install, the running release's on an upgrade off, own (chatd in this pod), external (another host's chatd) sandbox.mode off off, podman-socket, kubernetes (section 7) controller.conductor empty: off on a new install, the running release's on an upgrade a folder under the volume, an absolute path, or off controller.env TANDEM_NODE_AGENT: "off" the controller's variables (proxy.md): backends declared here are locked on the page mcpBridge.* off a stdio MCP server as HTTP on the pod's loopback (section 8) ingress.*, networkPolicy.*, trust.* off section 5

The page's switches (Chat, the conductor) are stored in the config database on the volume. Once one was used, it wins over chat.mode and controller.conductor. An empty chat.mode or controller.conductor keeps what the running release has, so an upgrade to a chart with other defaults flips nothing. helm template and client-side dry runs cannot read the running release: they render the new-install default. Set both values explicitly in a release's values file when its renders are checked before an upgrade.

docs.title: 7. Chat and its sandboxes
docs.text:
chat.mode:

  • off (a new install): no chatd; the Chat tab says Chat is off. Switched on from the page, chatd runs in this pod with the chart's chatd.env (data in data/chat).
  • own: chatd runs in this pod from the start, a child of the controller. A pod restart ends the chat runs that are open (they come back interrupted; Continue resumes them).
  • external: another host runs chatd; the Chat tab forwards to QSE_CHAT_URL (controller.env).

sandbox.mode:

mode what needs off no sandbox runtime: chat runs without its sandbox tools and says so nothing podman-socket a rootless Podman socket on the node, mounted into the pod ops/sandbox/install.sh on the node; persistence.hostPath.path equal to persistence.mountPath (the runtime binds host paths); the socket's ACL open to uid 10001 kubernetes each chat's sandbox is a pod in this namespace (chatd/k8s.py) chat.mode own or off; the items below

For kubernetes:

  1. Access. The chart makes a Role (pods: get, list, watch, create, delete; pods/exec; pods/log; this namespace only) and gives its token to the controller container only. The sandbox pods run as their own account, with no Role and no token.
  2. Network. Two NetworkPolicies: a sandbox pod reaches only chatd's egress proxy port (sandbox.kubernetes.egressPort, 3128) on the controller's pod, and nothing reaches it. At each start chatd runs a probe pod that tries the controller's port and the API; when either answers, the cluster does not enforce NetworkPolicy and chatd offers no sandbox. Its log says the cluster check passed, or why not.
  3. Isolation. hostUsers: false (the default) gives each sandbox pod a user namespace and a 512-process limit per pod. Set true where the cluster cannot (the node's podPidsLimit is then the only process limit). runtimeClassName takes gVisor or Kata where the cluster has one.

  4. The image. tandem-sandbox:1 is built in the cluster and imported into each node's containerd; nothing is pushed or pulled (imagePullPolicy: Never). Per node, amd64 and arm64 alike:

    bash ops/sandbox/build-k8s.sh tandemapp user@node # MicroK8s bash ops/sandbox/build-k8s.sh tandemapp user@node --ctr "ctr -n k8s.io"

    A kaniko Job on that node builds ops/sandbox/Containerfile for its architecture and writes a tar to a host folder; the script imports it over SSH (sudo -n). The node needs the internet for the build only. Check it: sudo microk8s ctr images ls | grep tandem-sandbox. 5. Files. A sandbox's /workspace and /home/agent are subPaths of the release's volume (data/chat/workspaces/<chat>, data/chat/homes/<chat>), so the sandbox pods run on the controller's node. chatd (uid 10001) and the sandbox (uid 1000) both get access through POSIX ACLs on the chat's two folders. 6. Limits. memoryGiB (2), cpus (4) and maxRunning (2) per release, counted from the cluster's pods.

    The values for sandbox pods:

    chat:
  mode: own
sandbox:
  mode: kubernetes
  kubernetes:
    image: tandem-sandbox:1
    imagePullPolicy: Never
    hostUsers: false
    memoryGiB: "2"
    maxRunning: "2"

    After the upgrade, check one sandbox end to end: a chat that runs a shell command, a fetch from the internet through the egress proxy, and no sandbox pod left after the chat is deleted for good.

    Moving chat's data in. tandem-app chat-move brings an older chatd's data folder into data/chat (each file checked by sha256). A tar copy carries no ACLs: the first sandbox start of each moved chat sets them on its workspace and home once, which takes a while for a chat with tens of thousands of files; later starts set none.

docs.title: 8. The MCP bridge sidecar
docs.text:
mcpBridge serves a stdio MCP server (a program you put on the volume, with its own login folder) as streamable HTTP on the pod's loopback, for chatd's MCP servers (http://127.0.0.1:<port><path>):

mcpBridge:
  enabled: true
  name: tools
  port: 8031
  path: /mcp
  command: [/var/lib/tandemapp/mcp/bin/server, mcp]
  env:
    SERVER_HOME: /var/lib/tandemapp/mcp/home

The bridge must never take the controller down. Kubernetes counts a pod Ready only while all of its containers run, and the Service sends traffic to Ready pods only: a sidecar in CrashLoopBackOff makes the page and the API answer 503 for minutes, whatever the controller's state. So the bridge's container never exits (a loop starts the bridge again 5 s after it ends) and has no probe. Check it after an install or upgrade with an MCP initialize and tools/list from the controller container:

kubectl -n tandemapp exec deploy/tandemapp -c controller -- python3 -c '
import json, urllib.request as u
def call(m, i, p=None, s=None):
    h = {"Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream"}
    if s: h["Mcp-Session-Id"] = s
    r = u.urlopen(u.Request("http://127.0.0.1:8031/mcp", json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": i, "method": m, "params": p or {}}).encode(), h), timeout=60)
    return r.headers.get("Mcp-Session-Id"), r.read().decode()
s, _ = call("initialize", 1, {"protocolVersion": "2025-03-26", "capabilities": {}, "clientInfo": {"name": "check", "version": "1"}})
print(call("tools/list", 2, s=s)[1][:300])'

docs.title: 9. Upgrades and rollback
docs.text:
1. Build the new archive (section 2).

  2. Put it on the volume while the old release runs: copy it into incoming/ through the running controller container and check it there:

    kubectl -n tandemapp cp tandemapp-.tar.gz :/var/lib/tandemapp/incoming/tandemapp-.tar.gz -c controller kubectl -n tandemapp exec -c controller -- sha256sum /var/lib/tandemapp/incoming/tandemapp-.tar.gz

    (Or set release.archive.url; or copy it into the waiting init container after the upgrade, as on install.) 3. Note the revision: helm history tandemapp -n tandemapp. 4. helm upgrade tandemapp charts/tandemapp -n tandemapp -f values.yaml with the new release.id and sha256. The Deployment is Recreate (one volume, one pod): the API is down from the old pod's stop until the new one is Ready (longer when the init container unpacks a new release). 5. Check: rollout status, helm test, the pod's containers all Ready with 0 restarts, and watch it for a few minutes (the same pod, restarts unchanged, the page answering).

    From the admin token to accounts. Upgrade (leave auth.mode and auth.bootstrap empty). The Secret keeps its name, key and value: the old admin token works once as the setup code, and once an owner exists (made with it, or from the controller's admin password) it is an API token, from that moment and with no restart, for scripts that ends after 30 days, marked for review. It never signs in to the page. Keep the Secret while you may roll back: helm rollback to the revision before brings back the template that reads it as the admin token, which signs in there as before. A network- reachable release with no admin password answers 401 everywhere after this upgrade until the setup code is used.

    helm rollback tandemapp <revision> -n tandemapp goes back. The old release's folder is still on the volume, so no archive is needed. Releases are never removed by the chart: remove old releases/<id> folders by hand once you will not roll back to them.

docs.title: 10. Troubleshooting
docs.text: what you see why, and what to do the pod stays Init:0/1 the init container waits for the archive: kubectl logs <pod> -c release says the path; copy it in (section 4). sha256 differs: the file or the value is wrong the page and the API answer 503, the controller's log is fine a container of the pod is not running, so the pod is not Ready: kubectl get pod (READY, RESTARTS) and kubectl describe pod. Never give a sidecar a tcpSocket or httpGet probe on a port it binds on loopback only: the kubelet probes the pod's address, the probe fails forever, and the sidecar's restarts take the Service down Chat says "Chat is off" it is: switch it on in Settings → App, or set chat.mode: own (the page's switch wins once used) chats run without sandbox tools sandbox.mode is off, or chatd's start check found isolation missing: the controller's log and <volume>/state/logs/chatd.log say which (NetworkPolicy not enforced, a runtimeClass that does not exist, the image not on the node) a moved chat's first sandbox start is slow the one ACL pass over its files (section 7) every client is throttled after a few wrong passwords they share the ingress's address (section 5) accounts mode: every route answers 401, also through kubectl port-forward no owner yet: use the setup code (section 3); users setup-code through kubectl exec makes a new one the health page says exposure_plain_http behind a TLS ingress auth.trustedProxy does not cover the ingress controller's address (section 5) an OpenAI client gets 503 through the ingress ingress.api.openai is false: unset it an OpenAI client with a token gets 403 api_not_exposed the OpenAI API is "this machine" on the page's API exposure switch: set it to "network" /chat-engine answers from outside the Ingress is not the chart's, or a proxy in front routes around it: block the path there too

docs.title: TandemApp in one command, or in one container
docs.text: The overview, the first page, upgrades and backups: install.md.

docs.title: One command
docs.text:
A release archive carries the built page, so a host installs TandemApp with Python 3.11 or newer alone: Linux on arm64 or x86_64 (a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 too), or macOS. No root, no Node, no git.

tar -xzf tandemapp-<version>.tar.gz
bash tandemapp-<version>/packaging/install.sh

It prints each step, then the URL (http://127.0.0.1:8080/). What it does:

  1. Checks the page in the archive against its bundle.json.
  2. Copies the release to ~/.local/share/tandemapp/releases/<version>-<hash> and points current at it.
  3. Makes one venv with this host's Python and cryptography and psutil (never torch). The same Python and dependencies share one venv across releases.
  4. Writes the state dir ~/.tandemllm (0700): a fresh master key secrets.key (0600) and app.env (0600) with the address and port, TANDEM_CHAT=off, TANDEM_CONDUCTOR=off and TANDEM_NODE_AGENT=off. Also chatd.env (2 GiB and 2 running sandboxes), read once Chat is on.
  5. Starts the controller: a systemd user unit tandem-app on Linux, a launchd agent org.tandemllm.app on macOS, or a background process where neither answers (a container, a shell without a user bus).
  6. Waits until /health names this release and its page.

Run it again to update. An unchanged release keeps running; a new one is switched to and restarted, and switched back when it does not come up. app.env keeps what it holds.

option what --listen ADDR the address to bind: 0.0.0.0, :: or one of the host's. An address beyond loopback writes no secret and prints a one-time setup code (below) --behind-proxy a reverse proxy or tunnel on this host sends other devices here: with accounts, this machine's browser is never trusted without a password (TANDEM_LOCAL_MODE=off) and the summary prints a setup code --port N default 8080 --chat off\|own\|external who runs chatd. A new app.env gets off; the page switches it later. own here runs chatd on this host from the start --with-sandbox Linux, sudo once: rootless Podman for chat's sandboxes (below). It switches nothing on --service auto\|systemd\|launchd\|process\|none how it runs (default: what the host has) --unit NAME, --launchd-label LABEL the systemd user unit's name (default tandem-app), the launchd job's label (default org.tandemllm.app). A second install on the same host needs its own name, --state-dir and --port --prefix DIR, --state-dir DIR where the releases and the state go --wheels DIR install the venv offline from a folder of wheels --venv DIR use a venv that is there --bundle-url URL --bundle-sha256 HEX, --build-page a tree without a built page: fetch one, or build it with Node 20.19 or newer --dry-run print what it would do

Nothing is changed when a unit or launchd job of that name runs another prefix or state dir, or when another listener holds the port: the install stops (exit 2) and names both.

On Linux a user unit stops at logout unless the user lingers; the install prints the one command (sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>).

docs.title: Sign-in with accounts
docs.text:
User accounts with roles, sessions and API tokens are the sign-in (there is no admin token and no open default any more; an older install's variables are named on the health page and can go once you will not roll back). auth.md has the roles, tokens and recovery steps.

  • This machine only (the default address, no proxy): local mode. The page opens without a password and offers "Set a password"; nothing else on the network reaches it. A tool on this machine needs no API key: a made-up one counts as none, and an API token as itself. The installer prints no code.
  • Beyond loopback (--listen), or behind a proxy (--behind-proxy): no local mode (TANDEM_LOCAL_MODE=off). Nobody signs in until the first owner is made. The installer's summary prints a one-time setup code and the address; open the page and enter it with the owner's name and password. The code is single use, valid 24 hours and spent after 5 wrong tries. While no owner exists each start of the controller logs a fresh one, and tandem-app users setup-code prints another.
  • A lost password: tandem-app users reset-password NAME on this machine prints a one-time code; sign in with it as the password, then set one. Whoever can read the state directory can do this, so no password is asked.
  • API exposure. The OpenAI-compatible API and the Messages API each have a switch on the page: "this machine" (the default) or "network". Other devices need a token and the switch on network; an install that had API keys starts with the OpenAI switch on network so its clients keep working. A controller on loopback is not reachable from other devices whatever the switch says: change the listen address too.
  • A proxy that ends TLS on another address: name it in TANDEM_TRUSTED_PROXY (addresses and CIDR ranges, IPv4 and IPv6, comma separated, e.g. 192.0.2.10,2001:db8::/64), or every API token through it counts as sent over plain HTTP. A bad entry is ignored and named on the health page.
  • tandem-app service install --host 0.0.0.0 refuses while no owner has a password, unless --setup-code, which prints a code. tandem-app check says where the sign-in stands.
  • An install that had the admin token keeps it working for scripts for 30 days, as an API token marked for review. It never signs in to the page. auth.md lists the old variables; remove them from app.env once you will not go back to an older release. The health page names each one still set.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text: Keep the controller on loopback and let the proxy end TLS. Forward everything to http://127.0.0.1:8080, with streaming on and long timeouts (an answer can take minutes): in nginx proxy_buffering off, proxy_read_timeout 3600s, proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr, client_max_body_size 200m. Do not route /chat-engine: that is chatd's way to the gateway on the same host. Set an admin password before the page is reachable from another machine; with accounts install with --behind-proxy, so the proxy's requests are never taken for this machine. A proxy that forwards only some paths must still send TandemApp every prefix in install.md; proxy.md has the rest.

docs.title: Chat's sandboxes
docs.text:
Chat works without a sandbox runtime: its files, shell and browser tools are off, and the page says so. For sandboxes on Linux:

bash tandemapp-<version>/packaging/install.sh --with-sandbox

runs ops/sandbox/install.sh with sudo once: rootless Podman under its own user tandem-sbx with its socket, the sandbox image, an nftables table that keeps that user off private and loopback addresses, and POSIX ACLs on chatd's folders. chatd.env gets the socket's path. Then switch Chat on from the page.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) or Ubuntu on a Pi 4 or 5 with 8 GB or more. Install the venv module first: sudo apt install python3 python3-venv.
  • Sandboxes need the kernel's memory controller. Raspberry Pi OS ships it off. The install (and the health page, no_memory_cgroup) says so; the fix is to add cgroup_enable=memory cgroup_memory=1 to the one line of /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt and reboot. Nothing edits boot files for you.
  • Rebuilding the sandbox image later needs the egress table off for the build (its resolver is on loopback): sudo systemctl stop tandem-sbx-nft, build as tandem-sbx, then start it again.
  • Keep the state dir on an SSD rather than the SD card (--state-dir).

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: The install runs a launchd agent; its log is ~/.tandemllm/logs/tandem-app.log. macOS asks once whether the controller may use the local network (Add engine's LAN search needs it). A controller that launchd starts gets no such prompt: the App page shows the state and the way around it (type the engine's address, or run the controller on a Linux host). --with-sandbox is Linux only; on a Mac, name Docker Desktop's socket in chatd.env (QSE_SANDBOX_SOCKET=...). A Mac that sleeps stops the API: the page warns while a Mac runs the controller.

docs.title: From a checkout
docs.text: python3 tools/app_release.py pack --out tandemapp-<version>.tar.gz makes the archive from a tree with a built page (python3 tools/dashboard_bundle.py build builds it with Node). The same tree packs to the same bytes.

docs.title: The container
docs.text:
packaging/Dockerfile.app builds an image on python:3.12-slim with the page (built in a Node stage) and the OpenSSH client, and no compiler or torch:

docker build -f packaging/Dockerfile.app -t tandemllm-app .
docker run -d --name tandem-app --network host -v tandem-app:/data \
    -e TANDEM_HOST=127.0.0.1 tandemllm-app

--network host lets Add engine find the engines the LAN advertises. Behind a published port (-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080) you type the engine's address instead. Inside the container the server binds 0.0.0.0 unless TANDEM_HOST says otherwise. A container never gets local mode: nothing answers without a sign-in, and the first log lines hold a setup code that makes the owner (docker logs tandem-app).

Everything it keeps is in /data. A new /data starts bare: Chat and the conductor off. The start script records its choice once in /data/container.env; -e TANDEM_CHAT=own overrides it, and the page's switch overrides both. A /data that an older image made keeps Chat on. Chat in the container needs a runtime's socket for its sandboxes:

docker run ... -v /var/run/docker.sock:/run/tandem/sandbox.sock --group-add <the socket's gid>

or a rootless Podman socket, with --user its owner. Without one, chat runs without its sandbox tools and the health page says so. The System view sees the container, not the host: add --pid=host, or run tandem-app hostcollect on the host.

To build the image yourself from a checkout and run it:

docker build -f packaging/Dockerfile.app -t tandemllm-app app
cp packaging/app.env.example app.env  # fill in; no quotes around values
docker run -d --name tandem-app -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -v tandem-app:/data \
    --env-file app.env tandemllm-app

docs.title: Installing TandemApp
docs.text: TandemApp is the controller in front of your engines: the gateway (one OpenAI-compatible API), the usage ledger, the fleet and the page. It needs no GPU and no engine on its own host. This page says which way to install it, what each way gives you, and what comes after the install. Each way has its own page with the steps.

docs.title: Which way
docs.text:
way for needs page one command a Linux box (arm64 or x86_64, a Raspberry Pi too) or a Mac Python 3.11 or newer; no root, no Node, no git install-linux.md one container any host with Docker or Podman a container runtime install-linux.md Helm a Kubernetes cluster Kubernetes 1.27 or newer (1.33 for sandbox pods), a storage class, an ingress controller install-kubernetes.md

All three run the same code and the same page, and start the same way: bare.

docs.title: From a checkout
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/TandemLLM/TandemApp.git && cd TandemApp
pip install '.[host]'  # the host extra adds psutil and NVML for the System view
tandem-app                 # http://127.0.0.1:8080/dashboard/ opens on Setup

With backends declared in an env file instead of the page:

cat > app.env <<'EOF'
TANDEM_BACKENDS=vllm1
TANDEM_BACKEND_VLLM1_KIND=vllm
TANDEM_BACKEND_VLLM1_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1
EOF
tandem-app check --env-file app.env        # prints what would run, writes nothing
tandem-app serve --env-file app.env

A first backend from the command line, a cloud API with its key, and one request through it:

printf 'TANDEM_BACKENDS=deepseek\nTANDEM_BACKEND_DEEPSEEK_KIND=deepseek\nTANDEM_BACKEND_DEEPSEEK_KEY=
    "$DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" > app.env && chmod 600 app.env
tandem-app serve --env-file app.env &
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model": "deepseek-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi"}]}'

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/dashboard/#/usage: the request is one row there, with its tokens, its time to first token and its cost at the model's price. backends.md has a section for each kind of backend.

docs.title: What a new install runs
docs.text:
A new TandemApp runs only the gateway in front of the engines you pair (OPS-288):

  • no backend until you pair an engine host or add a server;
  • Chat off: no chatd, no sandbox runtime needed, and the Chat tab says "Chat is off";
  • the conductor off: no profiles, router, packages, notes or decision model in front of the backends;
  • no MCP server, no hook, no plugin.

Each part is switched on from the page: Settings → App → What runs here. Every switch first shows what it changes and asks to confirm. The switch is stored in the controller's config database and wins over the install's setting from then on. An install that set a value itself (TANDEM_CHAT=own in app.env, chat.mode: own in Helm values) keeps it: a default changed in a later release never flips a running install.

part on off Chat chatd runs on the controller's host (its data in the state dir); with no sandbox runtime chat works without its sandbox tools, and the page says so chatd stops (a chat that runs ends interrupted, Continue resumes it later); the chats stay Conductor the harness in front of the backends, from the next request; its documents in the folder TANDEM_CONDUCTOR names, else <state dir>/conductor every backend relayed as it is; the documents stay

The engine's own chat mode (the conductor and chat extension inside an engine) is the engine's setting. The same page lists the engine hosts paired over SSH and switches each one (tandem remote mode set engine|chat on the host does the same). It also lists what is connected (backends, and Chat's MCP servers while Chat is on), each with disable and remove.

docs.title: The first page
docs.text:
Open the URL the install prints (http://127.0.0.1:8080/ for the one command). A TandemApp with no engine opens the setup wizard:

  1. Add engine. It lists the engines the LAN advertises (mDNS _tandem._tcp), or takes an address you type (a tailnet name too).
  2. Pair. On the engine host, tandem pair prints a 6-digit code, the SSH host key's fingerprint and the address. Type the code. The code authenticates the host key: nothing is trusted on first use. A code is good for 5 minutes and 5 tries, and works once. The other ways: a password used once (never stored), or a key line to paste.
  3. Model. The bare engine is preselected; pick a model and follow its download.
  4. First answer. With Chat on, the message goes to the Chat tab. With Chat off (the default), the Playground asks the engine through the gateway, or the page switches Chat on.

Each engine host gets its own SSH key pair, sealed with the controller's master key. Pairing needs the admin from another machine: set an admin password first (Settings → App), or pair from the controller's own host. More engines: Settings → Add engine. A Spark with TandemNode, or any OpenAI-compatible server by its URL: Settings → Get started.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
A reverse proxy in front of TandemApp must send it every path the controller owns, not only the data plane. The page calls all of them from the same address: a proxy that sent /v1/settings or /v1/fleet/ to an engine leaves the Settings, Hooks, Decision providers, Plugins and Health pages with the engine's 404 (OPS-292). The simple setup forwards everything to TandemApp and blocks /chat-engine and /plugin-backends. A proxy that also fronts an engine on the same address sends TandemApp every prefix it answers always, a "both" prefix while its condition holds, and the rest to the engine.

"Both" means TandemApp and an engine each answer the path for their own state. TandemApp answers /v1/conductor, /v1/library and the session addresses only while its own conductor is on (Settings → App → What runs here; a new install has it off); an engine answers them only through the extension that runs the conductor in its process, and its engine-only screens are under /v1/engine. proxy.md says when the data plane goes to TandemApp. Block /plugin-backends even when the proxy runs on TandemApp's own host: the controller takes it from loopback only, and a proxy there connects from loopback.

prefix answered by TandemApp answers it what / TandemApp always redirects to the page /dashboard and below TandemApp always the page and its files /v1/fleet and below TandemApp always the fleet: nodes, engine hosts, deployments, health, hooks, decision providers, plugins, the App page, the gateway for a page whose /v1 is an engine's /v1/settings and below TandemApp always the settings interface: every scope, change sets, versions, the audit /v1/config and below TandemApp always the Backends and Setup screens: backends, rules, prices, users /v1/auth and below TandemApp always the sign-in, the first-run setup, sessions and accounts /v1/chat-app and below TandemApp always the Chat tab: chatd behind the controller (off, own or external) /v1/collect and below TandemApp always a plugin's or a host collector's batches, with its own token /plugin-panels and below TandemApp always a running plugin's panels, in the page's frame /v1/chat/completions both always the data plane: TandemApp's gateway (proxy.md says when a proxy sends it to TandemApp or to an engine) /v1/completions both always the data plane /v1/embeddings both always the data plane /v1/responses both always the data plane /v1/messages and below TandemApp always the data plane in the Messages API: a message, count_tokens; an engine answers 404 /v1/models and below both always the data plane: the model list and one model's card /v1/cache/peek both when a deployment routes the cache routed to the member of a Replicas deployment that holds the conversation /v1/cache/prewarm both when a deployment routes the cache as peek /v1/cache/release both when a deployment routes the cache as peek /v1/cache and below an engine never an engine's cache routes; clear is the engine's only /v1/dashboard and below both always summary, usage, requests, live, logs, metrics, the page's sign-in: TandemApp's own ledger (a page whose /v1/dashboard reaches an engine reads TandemApp's under /v1/fleet/ledger, proxy.md) /v1/conductor and below both when its conductor is on the conductor's documents, journal, sessions and memory notes; an engine answers it only through the extension that runs the conductor in its process, and the engine-only screens are /v1/engine /v1/library and below both when its conductor is on the package library /v1/laya and below both when its conductor is on and the decider role names a Laya endpoint Laya for scripts /s and below both when its conductor is on a session's address: /v1/library and /v1/laya under its token; /v1/memory under it is the engine's only /health both always liveness: each answers its own /metrics both always Prometheus: each answers its own /v1/engine and below an engine never the engine-only screens: deciders, narrator, shadow, disk tier, residency, pairing /v1/setup and below an engine never an engine's Setup Guide; through TandemApp: /v1/fleet/nodes//setup /v1/memory and below an engine never the model's own memory under a session's address /v1/tokenize an engine never the engine's tokenizer /v1/systemone an engine never the engine's decision wire /v1/replica and below an engine never a replica's identity /readyz an engine never the engine's readiness /metrics/up an engine never the engine's up gauge /_tandem and below an engine never the engine's status responder while it restarts /chat-engine and below nobody: block it never chatd's way to the gateway on the controller's own host: block it at the proxy /plugin-backends and below nobody: block it never a plugin's backend, for the controller's own gateway: it is taken from loopback only, and a proxy on the same host connects from loopback, so block it

The same list is machine-readable in controller-routes.json; tests/test_route_list.py checks it against the paths the page calls and the routes the controller answers. Streaming answers need buffering off and long timeouts at the proxy (install-linux.md, install-kubernetes.md).

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text:
way state what is in it one command ~/.tandemllm (--state-dir), mode 0700; releases in ~/.local/share/tandemapp (--prefix) app.env, config.sqlite3 (backends, routes, users, settings and the page's switches), ledger.sqlite3, fleet.sqlite3, secrets.key (the master key), admin.json (the admin password's hash), controller/ (its certificate, the engine hosts' SSH keys and pins), chatd.env, chat/ once Chat ran, conductor/ once the conductor ran, logs/ container the /data volume the same, plus container.env (the chat mode its first start chose) Helm one ReadWriteOnce volume at /var/lib/tandemapp state/ (the same files), data/chat, conductor/, releases/<id> and current, ca/, home/, incoming/, backups/

Each page's window layout per device class is kept in the config database too (layouts/<page>); the last write wins.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
• One command: unpack the new release archive and run its packaging/install.sh again. It switches to the new release, restarts, and switches back when the new one does not answer /health. The old releases stay. app.env keeps its values; only --listen, --port and --chat change it.
  • Container: pull or build the new image and recreate the container on the same volume.
  • Helm: helm upgrade with the new release.id and archive; helm rollback goes back. See install-kubernetes.md.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Stop the controller, or copy the SQLite files with sqlite3 <file> ".backup <copy>" while it runs, and keep the whole state dir (or volume) together. secrets.key is the master key: without it the stored API keys, the engine hosts' keys and chat's MCP secrets cannot be read. Keep it apart from the copies, the way you keep any key. The page's export (Settings → App → Fleet configuration) is a file of the registry without any secret: good for a record, not a backup.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
• One command: systemctl --user disable --now tandem-app and remove ~/.config/systemd/user/tandem-app.service (Linux), or launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/org.tandemllm.app and remove ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.tandemllm.app.plist (macOS); an install made with --unit or --launchd-label uses that name instead (the install's summary prints its stop command). Then remove the prefix folder. The state dir stays until you remove it.
  • Container: docker rm -f tandem-app; the volume stays until docker volume rm.
  • Helm: helm uninstall; the volume's claim stays (persistence.keep) until you delete it.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• install-linux.md: the one command, a Raspberry Pi, macOS, the container.
  • install-kubernetes.md: Helm, the release archive, sandboxes as pods.
  • ../charts/tandemapp/README.md: the chart's values.
  • proxy.md: the gateway, its configuration and every variable.
  • chat.md: Chat and its sandboxes.

docs.title: Memory notes
docs.text: The model keeps notes about the user and the work, as files, and reads them back in later turns and sessions. One note is one markdown file with a frontmatter: one fact, a title of at most 120 characters, a body of at most 400 words. The files are the truth; the dashboard's Memory screen (Notes tab) reads and edits them.

docs.title: Where the files are
docs.text:
~/.qwen38-spark-engine/memory/notes/<user>/
  INDEX.md                               generated each night: one line per live note
  user/<kind>-<slug>--<id>.md            about the person
  projects/<name>-<hash8>/<kind>-...md   about one working directory
  sessions/<session>/<kind>-...md        true for one conversation only
  revisions/<id>/<n>.md                  every earlier text of a note
  archive/<yyyy-mm>/...                  archived notes, deleted after 30 days
  usage.json                             how often each note went into a request, by day

<user> is owner on the engine. A request the proxy relayed carries the proxy user's name (the key's label in process, X-Tandem-User from a loopback address or one listed in QWEN38_MEMORY_PROXIES); a relayed request without one reads and writes nothing. Files are 0600, and the store refuses a root inside a git work tree, as the transcripts do.

TandemLLM serves one user. Every client that reaches the engine (opencode, Open WebUI, a script with curl) is that user, so a "remember that ..." from any of them is a note in the same store and is read back in the next conversation; that is the intended behaviour, not a leak. A write is never silent: the answer carries the state line › remembered: <title> (or forgot, proposed) in its content, after the answer text, in every client (opencode shows it as the title of a reasoning part, its state-line channel), and the Notes screen lists each note with its writer and the request that wrote it, where it is archived or deleted.

A request that must not touch the notes says so with the header X-Tandem-Memory: off reads nothing, writes nothing and gets no memory card (the journal row has extra.memory = {mode: off, why: header}); read gets the reads as the profile gives them, no card, and a block the model writes anyway is hidden from the answer and dropped (journaled read_only). Tests, benchmarks and smoke checks against a live engine send X-Tandem-Memory: off. Any other value, or no header, leaves the profile's memory switch in charge (SRV-173, 2026-10-06: a self-test's curl "remember that my dog is called Biscuit" was recalled in the next conversation).

The eight kinds: rule (how the user wants things done), ruling (a decision), gotcha (what went wrong once), runbook, program_state (with verify_by; stale after that date and never injected), reference, registry, archive.

docs.title: How the model writes
docs.text:
It writes a block in its answer, usually after its text:

<tandem_memory op="add" scope="project" kind="gotcha">
title: the build needs node 20
tags: build

npm run build fails on node 18 with "Unexpected token 'with'".
</tandem_memory>

op is add, update (with id:) or archive (with id: and reason:). The server holds the block back from the client the way it holds a <tool_call> (tandemapp/memblock.py), writes the note, and the client sees one state line, › remembered: the build needs node 20, when the profile shows state lines. The line goes into the content, after the answer, whatever the profile's state-line channel and the request's reasoning_format (0.3.43-test, SRV-185: in tags a line after </think> had no place and was dropped, and a reasoning_content line after the answer went unseen, so Open WebUI and the OpenAI SDK never showed a write); opencode's inline channel keeps it as a reasoning part's title. The server takes the line out of the history a client sends back, so the model never reads it. With X-Tandem-Memory: off or read nothing is written and no line is shown. A closed block never reaches the client, whether it was written or not (SRV-277, 0.4.5-test): one over 2,000 characters, the fifth of an answer, or one the store refused is hidden like a written one, and its reason goes to the journal (memory_notes/write, the row's extra.memory.failed) and the log line [memory] <request>: 1 block(s) not written (cap), hidden from the answer; its tokens are hidden spans, so the next turn still resumes at the end anchor. Before, a refused block went out as the markup it was: an Open WebUI chat showed <tandem_memory scope="project" ...> to the user. Only text that is not a closed block goes out as written: a block that never closed, one still open after 4,000 characters, <tandem_memoryx. A block inside the reasoning is left alone.

With a chat's tools in view the model may write the note as a tool call, <tool_call><function=tandem_memory>... or the JSON form. No client offers that tool, so the server takes the call as the block it means (tandemapp/memblock.py, the parser the background writer uses): written or refused as the block is, hidden, never a call the client gets. Other calls in the same answer go out as usual. An answer that is only notes goes on after a hidden result (the monitor's E1, case M), so the client gets the model's answer instead of an empty turn. The switches above apply to the call as to the block, and a client that offers its own tandem_memory tool gets its calls.

A conversation without a working directory (every Open WebUI chat, a script with curl) has no project. A scope="project" add there is written at user scope (rescoped: project in the result and the journal), since every client is the one user and a note is meant to be read back in the next conversation (SRV-173); a session note would be gone in the next chat. Before 0.4.5-test it was refused (no_project).

The rules are code, not prompt text (tandemapp/conductor/notes.py):

  • A write over a cap is refused, never cut: title 120 characters, body 400 words, 20 notes a session, 500 live notes a user.
  • Every title and body passes the secret-pattern refusal of the transcripts; a body that is mostly a secret is refused.
  • A rule or ruling about the user needs the user's own message in the turn. A tool turn or a script cannot write one.
  • One written in a tool turn is kept at session scope instead, provisional, for that conversation only (demoted: rule_from_tool in the journal); without a session it is refused.
  • The model writes provisional notes. Ratify, pin and delete are the dashboard's. A model revision of a ratified note makes it provisional again, and so does the model's archive of one: the note stays, with the model's reason in its changelog, until the user archives it or ratifies it again on the Notes tab. The client sees no forgot line for it.
  • Before an add lands, the same scope is searched: the same normalised title, or one of BM25's top 5 whose word overlap is at or above dedupe_threshold (0.6), turns the add into a revision of that note.

The model's scripts have the same write as a route, under the session's address only: POST {tandem_url}/v1/memory, GET {tandem_url}/v1/memory/search?q=, GET {tandem_url}/v1/memory/<id> (server/memory_api.py). Without a known session token the routes answer 403.

The rules are code, not prompt text (tandemapp/conductor/notes.py).

flowchart LR
    block["a <tandem_memory> block in an answer"] --> checks
    writer["the writer's hidden turn"] --> checks
    script["a script: POST /v1/memory"] --> checks
    checks["checks<br/>caps refuse, never cut<br/>secret patterns refused<br/>a rule needs the user's words<br/>same fact: a revision"] --> prov["note, provisional<br/>one fact, one file"]
    checks -.-> refused["refused: the text goes out as it was"]
    prov -- a person --> rat["ratified, pinned<br/>on the Notes tab"]
    prov -- archive --> arch["archived<br/>deleted after 30 days"]
    prov --> reads["read back<br/>the card, the index, matching notes"]
    rat --> reads

The life of a memory note. Three ways in, one set of checks, a provisional note that a person may ratify or pin, reads back into later turns, and an archive.

docs.title: How the model reads
docs.text:
A profile's memory switch: none (nothing at all: no card, no note, the request is the release's; a profile stored without the key reads the same), off (as none, and one note a session tells the model that memory is off in this profile, so it says so instead of claiming it has no memory), shadow (the card goes in and blocks are written, nothing is read back) or on. Every shipped profile sets it (SRV-703): on in chat, coding, hermes and chat-app, none in general, tools, overnight and the locked raw and bench. With on, three tail notes, each replayed at its place on later turns so each costs its prefill once:

  • the memory card, about 150 tokens: the block's shape and when to write one;
  • the index, on the first turn of a session and again after a compaction: the pinned ratified rules, then one line per note the request may see (settings.memory.notes.index_tokens, 1,500). index_order recent (the default) lists the scopes in turn, pinned, ratified, newest first; ranked picks the lines across the scopes by their BM25 score against the turn's message, pinned first, so a smaller index_tokens keeps the notes the message is about (SPD-249). With QWEN38_NOTES_HEAD=on (off by default) a conversation's first turn carries the memory card, a recent index and the class note at the end of the system message (one the conductor adds when the client sent none), each block unchanged, and the prefill's grid is cut where they end (engine/cache.py Grid), so chats of one user share that head in the prefix cache; a ranked index, the bodies and every later note stay at the last message's end.
