Moving it to a Spark reads a plan first (GET /v1/fleet/controller/move?to=<node>&port=: the new API URL, each node and what happens to it, what stays) and runs with the plan's confirm:

  1. the fleet's export: the config database without its secrets, the wizard's sessions and the jobs (backends, routes, the proxy's keys as hashes, rules, nodes with their pins, layouts), and each stored API key, to be stored again under the new controller's own master key;
  2. the Spark's TandemNode starts a controller there (POST /node/controller: a systemd user unit, its own state dir with the export, an env file and the password's hash as admin.json, all 0600; its first start makes that the account owner, and the password is never an admin token or an API token), which imports the export at its first start and makes its own certificate; a state dir that holds a controller's database already is refused;
  3. each paired node is handed to the new certificate by its current owner (PUT /node/owner): from then on the old controller is refused and the new one accepted. The Spark itself is released and read by the new controller over its loopback; a node reached through an SSH tunnel stays (its key is a file on this machine);
  4. the new controller is asked for the nodes until each answers it, the old controller's refusal is checked, and the old one says moved_to: its page follows to the new URL and the API URL is printed.

The metric history stays where it was. The way back starts on the machine that takes the fleet: its App settings take it from the controller's URL with that controller's admin password (POST /v1/fleet/controller/take); the giver seals its export to the taker's certificate (ECDH P-256, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM), the taker imports it, the giver hands its nodes over and says moved_to the taker. Every move, handover and take needs pairing's rights.

A host with no engine (SRV-841). The controller runs on any Linux host with Python 3.11 or newer, arm64 or x86_64, with no engine, no engine data folder, no GPU and no TandemNode there: its engines are fleet members reached over HTTP, controlled over SSH (proxy/enginectl.py) or through their TandemNode agent. packaging/linux/tandem-app.sh runs it from a checkout or a venv with the state dir ~/.tandemllm (TANDEM_APP_STATE) and the env file app.env there, and defaults TANDEM_NODE_AGENT and TANDEM_CONDUCTOR to off unless the environment or the env file sets them; packaging/linux/tandem-app.service is its systemd user unit. Such a controller takes the fleet with POST /v1/fleet/controller/take like any other. A take across hosts also: points a backend whose URL is the giver's loopback (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1) at the host the taker reached the giver at; carries the giver's old key list (its users table, with the users of the engine's database it read) as hashes, which the taker imports as API tokens under review, while accounts and API tokens stay with the giver; carries each engine host over SSH with its key pair and pinned host key inside the sealed export (the giver drops both once it hands the host over; a key line with from= on the engine host needs the new address); carries the deployments; and clears a moved_to the taker kept from giving a fleet away before, so the original controller takes its fleet back the same way.

What runs here (OPS-288, Settings, App, GET /v1/fleet/app/parts, code: proxy/appparts.py). A new install runs the gateway only. Chat and the conductor are switched on and off from the page: each switch answers its plan first (what changes, in words, and a confirm) and applies with that confirm (POST /v1/fleet/app/parts/{chat,conductor} {on, confirm}; 409 stale_plan when the state changed since). The switch is stored in the config database (parts.chat, parts.conductor; not in the fleet's export) and wins over TANDEM_CHAT and TANDEM_CONDUCTOR from then on; until it is used, the install's values decide, so a changed default never flips a running install. Chat on starts this controller's own chatd (an external install forwards again instead), off stops it as a hand stop and every chat route answers 503 chat_off. The conductor on runs the harness from the next request with its documents in TANDEM_CONDUCTOR's folder, else <state dir>/conductor; off relays every backend as it is. No restart either way. The page also lists the engine hosts paired over SSH with their own mode (POST /v1/fleet/engines/{id}/mode), the backends and Chat's MCP servers, each with disable and remove.

Chat on the controller's host. --chat (TANDEM_CHAT) says who runs chatd. off, what a new install writes: nobody, until the page switches Chat on. external, the default when unset: TandemNode or an engine's launchers on the engine host, and the controller forwards /v1/chat-app/* to QSE_CHAT_URL as before. own: the controller starts chatd on its own host, watches it (a dead chatd started again, at most 3 times a clock hour; a hand stop holds it) and forwards to it, with chatd's own env file <state dir>/chatd.env (TANDEM_CHAT_ENV, packaging/linux/chatd.env.example): chatd gets that file and the controller's PATH, HOME, locale and session variables only, never its admin token or keys, and calls the controller's own gateway as its engine unless the file names another (QSE_CHAT_ENGINE). GET /v1/fleet/chat says what runs; POST /v1/fleet/chat/{start,stop,restart} acts (code: proxy/appchat.py). Under systemd chatd runs in a scope of its own, so a controller restart leaves its chat runs alone and the next start adopts it.

chatd off the engine host (SRV-843). chatd's engine is <the controller's URL>/chat-engine (code: proxy/chatengine.py): the gateway for the completions and the model list, the controller's conductor for the library and a user's skills, and the chat engine's own /health, /v1/dashboard/system, live rows, cache routes and tokenizer, so chatd's run slots still follow the engine's lanes. The chat engine is TANDEM_CHAT_ENGINE_BACKEND, else the default backend when it is a TandemLLM engine, else the first one. A user's skill goes into the conductor's packages document as an inline body, never by a path into skill_dirs. QSE_CHAT_HOST (app when the chat engine runs on another host, which the controller works out) sizes the sandboxes for a small host, 2 GiB and 2 running, and stops chatd from asking a remote engine to release memory; beside an engine they stay 4 GiB and 4. Once the controller has users, chatd gets a key of its own (user chatd, kept in its data folder). tandem-app chat-move --from USER@HOST:PATH moves an old chatd's data folder here: the old chatd stopped first, each file checked by sha256, the MCP servers' secrets sealed again with this host's master key, the old folder left untouched (code: proxy/chatmove.py). An engine on API 1.9 that wants its HTTP token from other hosts gets it from the data plane: tandem remote token rotate over SSH puts it in a sealed store per engine host, and every call to a TandemLLM backend on that host carries it (SRV-839).

The fleet update (Sparks → Update fleet, /v1/fleet/update, code: proxy/fleetupdate.py, the node's half proxy/nodeupdate.py). One release on every node: the one in the package this controller installs (tandem-app package, or TANDEM_NODE_WHEEL). The plan orders the nodes: those that serve nothing first, then each Replicas member alone (drained, updated, rejoined while another member serves its model), then nodes with a deployment only they serve (the plan names the downtime), then each Split's members together. A Split never updates partly: a member that cannot be updated refuses the Split, and a selection with one member and not another is refused 409 partial_split. An engine installer the controller cannot read (TANDEM_ENGINE_INSTALL_SH), or an engine ref that names no release (TANDEM_ENGINE_REF, the VERSION beside the installer), blocks the plan too, and its POST is refused 409 conflict before any node drains. On a node the agent takes the wheel (sha256 checked), installs it into its own virtual environment with pip, runs the engine's runtime install (the controller's TANDEM_ENGINE_INSTALL_SH with --runtime-only, at the same engine ref as Add Spark; skipped with "the controller sent no engine installer (TANDEM_ENGINE_INSTALL_SH)" when the controller has none; simulated on a virtual node) and replaces itself with the new code (same process id). The job keeps each node's phase in the config database; a controller restarted during it resumes where it was. A node that runs outside a virtual environment of its own (a checkout) is skipped with the words to update it by hand.

Mixed versions. The rule version-mismatch fires one alert for the fleet once the nodes that answer run more than one release for 60 s (a local build label counts as its release); it is held while an update runs. The fleet pill and the Overview say it, and its action opens Update fleet.

docs.title: vLLM and SGLang: their own metrics
docs.text:
The proxy relays a backend of kind vllm or sglang like any OpenAI-compatible server, and it also reads the engine's own /metrics page every 15 s. That page holds what a relay cannot see. It says how many requests run and wait inside the engine and how full the KV cache is. It gives the prefix-cache hit rate and the engine's own time split of each request. Speculation and preemptions are on it too. The Performance view shows one card per such backend, the System view shows the same cards, and a backend's page under Backends shows its engine.

The names come from the source of vLLM v0.30.0 and SGLang v0.5.21, the releases current on 2026-10-04. Each engine has a name table in proxy/engines.py. A family the page does not have maps to nothing, and its tile says "not reported by this backend". The proxy skips a family the table does not know. A new release can cost a tile, never a failed read.

figure vLLM SGLang running, waiting vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting sglang:num_running_reqs, sglang:num_queue_reqs KV in use vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc (a fraction, 1 is full) sglang:token_usage, and tokens from sglang:num_used_tokens of sglang:max_total_num_tokens decode rate vllm:generation_tokens_total over the window sglang:generation_tokens_total over the window, and the engine's own sglang:gen_throughput prefix-cache hits vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total over vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total sglang:cached_tokens_total over sglang:prompt_tokens_total, and the engine's own sglang:cache_hit_rate TTFT vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds sglang:time_to_first_token_seconds queue, prefill, decode vllm:request_queue_time_seconds, ..._prefill_time_seconds, ..._decode_time_seconds sglang:queue_time_seconds; no prefill or decode histogram preemptions vllm:num_preemptions_total sglang:num_retracted_requests_total speculation vllm:spec_decode_num_drafts_total, ..._num_draft_tokens_total, ..._num_accepted_tokens_total, ..._num_accepted_tokens_per_pos_total{position}: acceptance and tokens per step over the window, and acceptance per draft position sglang:spec_accept_rate and sglang:spec_accept_length, gauges over SGLang's own last window

Window figures come from the first and the newest reading of the last 5 minutes. With one reading, or no traffic in the window, they are null. vLLM's families carry an engine label per data-parallel engine; the proxy adds them up and takes the mean of a fraction. SGLang reports its scheduler families from the first tensor-parallel rank only. With --enable-metrics-for-all-schedulers every rank reports the same numbers, so the proxy keeps rank 0 and drops the rest instead of counting them twice.

The proxy's own /metrics carries the mapped families as qse_backend_* with a backend label, qse_backend_info{backend,kind,version} and qse_backend_scrape_age_seconds. They never enter the engine's own families. The Performance view reads them from that page; the System view reads the same figures from the backend's engine block in the system body.

The flags each engine needs:

vLLM SGLang the metrics page always on --enable-metrics; without it /metrics answers 404 and the card says so cached tokens per request --enable-prompt-tokens-details --enable-cache-report reasoning tokens per request --reasoning-parser (the stream's field is delta.reasoning) --reasoning-parser; without it SGLang still sends reasoning_tokens: 0, which the proxy reads as null when the stream carried reasoning the version GET /version GET /server_info (/get_server_info before it), which also gives the speculative settings, the cache report and the reasoning parser

The proxy does not call either engine's /health. On SGLang it runs a one-token generation when the server is idle, and the health poll's GET /v1/models already says whether the server answers. After a failed read the proxy waits 30 s, then 60, then 120 s between tries; after a 404 it asks every 120 s.

Two more facts from the v0.30.0 source matter for later layers. vLLM removed guided_choice and the other guided_* fields: it still answers 200 but ignores them, so a constrained question must use structured_outputs: {"choice": [...]}. And vLLM takes a client's X-Request-Id as the request id (chatcmpl-<id>; the engine's internal id adds 8 random hex characters), while SGLang takes rid in the body instead.

docs.title: Inside vLLM and SGLang: the plugins and the launcher
docs.text:
The /metrics page gives totals. A single request's queue time, its prefill time and whether the scheduler preempted it are not on it. Two small packages in plugins/ run inside the engine and send those numbers per request to the proxy (layer L2). Install one into the engine's own Python environment; neither has a dependency:

pip install plugins/vllm        # tandemllm-vllm-plugin: vLLM loads it from vllm.stat_logger_plugins
pip install plugins/sglang      # tandemllm-sglang-plugin: SGLang loads it from sglang.srt.plugins

The engine needs two variables, TANDEM_COLLECT_URL (the proxy's /v1/collect/<backend id>) and TANDEM_COLLECT_TOKEN. The plugin keeps the last 10,000 finished requests and 300 one-second scheduler samples in memory and posts what is new once a second, or an empty batch every 10 s when the engine is idle. plugins/README.md lists what each one reads, the versions it was checked against, and what happens when a release does not fit.

One command does all of it, from nothing to a backend with L2 data:

tandem-app launch vllm --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B --port 8100 -- --max-model-len 32768
tandem-app launch sglang --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B --port 30000

launch creates the backend in the config database (kind, http://127.0.0.1:<port>/v1, host same), hands the engine the collect URL and the token, adds the flags the dashboard reads (--enable-prompt-tokens-details on vLLM, --enable-metrics and --enable-cache-report on SGLang), checks that the plugin is installed in the engine's Python, and then replaces itself with the engine, so the pid it records is the engine's. Without the plugin installed it says how to install it and starts the engine at L1. --dry-run prints the command, --collect-url names another proxy, and everything after -- goes to the engine unchanged. launch is optional: an engine started by hand with the plugin and the two variables gives the same data.

The proxy joins each item to the request's ledger row by an id it sends upstream. vLLM gets X-Request-Id: px-<hex> and reports chatcmpl-px-<hex>, the row's own id. SGLang gets rid in the body and reports it unchanged. A client that sets its own X-Request-Id or rid keeps it, and the join uses it. The row then holds the engine's own numbers:

column vLLM SGLang queue_ms queued_time the scheduler's queue duration prompt_ms (prefill) prefill_time forward entry to the end of prefill decode_ms, decode_tps decode_time; (tokens - 1) over it first token to the end; the same rate prefill_tps uncached prompt tokens over the prefill the same cached_tokens num_cached_tokens cached_tokens (device, host, storage) preemptions num_preemptions retractions engine_finish, corrupted the engine's finish reason, the NaN check the finish reason blocks, draft_tokens, draft_accepted null (vLLM counts speculation per step, not per request) verify passes, proposed and accepted drafts l2_join exact, or approximate the same

TTFT stays the proxy's own: it is what the client saw. An item usually arrives a second after its row; the ledger then sets the columns on the row in place (Ledger.amend, schema version 4). An item that comes first waits for its row. Either waits 10 minutes for the other and is then dropped and counted. A request the proxy cannot tag (the Responses API, SGLang with n above 1) is matched by time and token counts: the same backend, the same prompt and completion counts, ends within 3 s of each other, and only when exactly one row fits. Such a row says approximate, and the log has one line for it.

The backend's card shows "L2 plugin" while batches arrive and "L1 only" after 60 s without one, with the plugin and engine versions it last saw. Under the tiles it says how many rows got the engine's split, and over the last 5 minutes the preemptions, the KV evictions and, on vLLM, the acceptance per draft position. The proxy's /metrics adds qse_backend_plugin_age_seconds and qse_backend_plugin_joins{join}. A vLLM that loads the second entry point, tandem_stats_endpoint (vLLM loads an endpoint plugin only when VLLM_PLUGINS names it), also serves GET /tandem/stats. When nothing was pushed for 25 s the proxy reads that route every 2 s instead. Items carry sequence numbers, so a batch read twice counts once.

The collect token is TANDEM_COLLECT_TOKEN in the proxy's environment, or a random one the proxy stores in its config database at the first need. Every batch needs it, from loopback too. It lets its holder post numbers for a backend that exists, nothing else. The plugins send counts and times only, never a prompt, an answer or a token id.

Not tested yet on real engines: the night pass (tools/proxy_engines_check.sh --plugins) installs both plugins into the release images, checks that every row joins and that the plugin's sums over 12 requests equal the engine's own /metrics within 1 %, and measures the plugin's cost on vLLM: decode tok/s with and without it, three starts (without, with, without), 20 requests each, gate 1 %.

docs.title: Models, names and routing
docs.text:
GET /v1/models and GET /v1/models/{id} answer in the Messages API's shape when the request carries anthropic-version, or x-api-key without Authorization (SRV-881; with TANDEM_AUTH=accounts, a token sent that way): {data: [{type: "model", id, display_name, created_at, max_input_tokens, max_tokens, capabilities, lifecycle, ...}], has_more, first_id, last_id}, paged by limit (20 by default, 1 to 1000), after_id and before_id, with the same models under the same ids. created_at is when the backend's list first showed the model; capabilities has every leaf the API names, true only where the card says so (image input, thinking, effort levels). Every other request gets the answer below, unchanged.

GET /v1/models lists each backend's real models under their own ids (deepseek-flash, Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B), with owned_by set to the backend's id and a tandem block (backend, kind, label, upstream id, the provider's name of the model and its largest max_tokens, each null when the adapter has none, whether the backend is a cloud API, context length, switches). In the engine's server, TandemLLM stays the engine's own. When two backends serve one id, both are listed as <backend>/<model> and the bare id is not; the prefixed form is always accepted. A model can get a public id of its own in the GUI, and an output limit: the operator's comes first in max_output, before the provider's list and the adapter's table, and a discovery never overwrites it (a relayed vLLM model has neither of the other two).

What a provider's own model list says goes into the card. DeepSeek's GET /models (read 2026-10-17) gives each model a name (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, shown as "DeepSeek V4.1 Flash"), context_window (1,048,576), max_output_tokens (393,216), input_modalities (text, image on deepseek-flash; text on deepseek-v4-pro) and effort (supported_levels low, high, max; default_level high). The discovery every 10 minutes stores them per model; the card then carries capabilities: vision when the input kinds name image, effort_levels, effort_default and effort_off (the word that turns thinking off: DeepSeek's reasoning_effort: none). The Chat tab offers the provider's levels in its effort chip, sends reasoning_effort with one of them, and sends images (uploads and render_page screenshots) only to a model that reads them.

A model id a later discovery finds for the first time is stored disabled: it is not listed until it is turned on under Backends. The log says [proxy] deepseek: new model <id> in /models, disabled until it is turned on under Backends, and one push goes to the ntfy topic of the monitor's stall watchdog (its url, token_file and ca_file) when one is set. An id is new once; when it leaves the list and comes back, nothing is sent again. On 2026-10-17 deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 was in DeepSeek's list for a while at about 01:59 UTC and then gone.

Every relayed answer's system_fingerprint (OpenAI's and DeepSeek's name for the backend configuration that wrote it) goes into its ledger row (schema 10) and the request detail on Performance. The model id stays deepseek-flash while the snapshot behind it changes; a new fingerprint in the rows shows the change.

A request goes to, in this order: an explicit <backend>/ prefix, the first enabled routing rule whose glob matches the id, the one backend that serves it, else OpenAI's 404 model_not_found (which names the prefixed forms when two backends serve the id).

A backend or a single model may name fallbacks. On a connect error, a 429, 502 or 503, before any byte reached the client, the proxy tries the next backend at once, or the same one again after 1 s, then 2 s (or its Retry-After, up to 30 s). At most 2 tries again in all. After the first byte a failure is an error frame and [DONE]. The ledger row records the backend that answered, fallback_from, retries and the upstream status.

The proxy adds no limit of its own to how many requests a backend takes at once: a cloud API, vLLM or SGLang gets as many as clients send, and answers its own 429 or 503 when it is full (that answer goes to a fallback as any 429 or 503 does). A backend's max_inflight (a number from 1 to 4,096 on its form, or TANDEM_BACKEND_<ID>_MAX_INFLIGHT) is a cap you set yourself: past it a request goes to a fallback with room, else it gets 503 with Retry-After: 1. Empty, null or none is no limit, the default. Until 0.3.44-test every backend got 64 without asking; a stored 64 became none when the config file moved to schema 2. How many requests TandemLLM's own engine decodes at once is the engine's setting, not a backend's: QSE_PARALLEL in its serve.env (docs/parallel-requests.md), shown on the Backends screen under the engine's name. Timeouts per backend (local: connect 5 s, first byte 600 s, idle gap 120 s; cloud: 10, 120, 60 s) end a request with finish_reason: timeout and the kind in error_type. A client that leaves closes the upstream connection within a quarter second, so the backend stops generating. The standalone proxy (python -m proxy) closes a client's connection that sends nothing for 60 s while it reads a request, or sits idle that long between requests (--idle-timeout, TANDEM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_S; 0 for none). The timeout ends when the answer starts: a stream, the Chat tab's terminal included, is never cut by it.

docs.title: What the dashboard shows for a relayed request
docs.text:
Measured or null, never estimated:

figure from prompt, completion tokens the backend's usage; null when it sends none cached prompt tokens prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens (OpenAI; vLLM with --enable-prompt-tokens-details; SGLang with --enable-cache-report), prompt_cache_hit_tokens (DeepSeek), input_tokens_details.cached_tokens (Responses), cache_read_input_tokens (Anthropic-compatible) cache write tokens cache_creation_input_tokens (Anthropic-compatible); counted in the prompt tokens and paid once, at the model's cache write price (its input price without one) reasoning tokens completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens (vLLM with --reasoning-parser), SGLang's reasoning_tokens; a reported 0 beside streamed reasoning is null TTFT arrival at the proxy to the first frame with a token; the network and the backend's queue are inside it decode tok/s (completion tokens - 1) / (last token frame - first token frame); null without usage, because a frame is not a token cost the model's price when the row is written. One exception: a stream cut at its token's spend limit (finish limit) has no usage, so its row carries an estimate, computed from the frames sent so far (each frame one output token, at the output price; the prompt's part is not in it) proxy overhead arrival to the upstream send, plus the first frame's delay through the proxy

Queue, prefill time, blocks, draft acceptance and the cache source come off an engine's loop and are null for a relayed row; the views say "not reported by this backend". The Usage view filters by backend (engine is the engine's own rows) and by user, and shows the cost of the priced models. With a relayed backend in the ledger, Usage has a table of the engine and each relayed backend side by side (requests, tokens, decode and TTFT p50, cost), and Performance draws them apart: relayed requests are red dots of their own on a log axis in Recent requests, and a line of their own beside the engine's in the decode and TTFT history. The cache sources table and the engine's history count the engine's own requests only; the Live panel names a relayed request's backend and says its tokens are counted at its end.

docs.title: Every request at once: Performance, Parallel
docs.text:
With several backends, tens of streams run side by side. Performance has two pages: Engine (the engine's own requests, one at a time) and Parallel (#/performance?tab=parallel), which shows every request in flight on every backend, our engine included. It reads GET /v1/dashboard/parallel once a second (tandemapp/parallel.py, contract parallel.schema.json); the server builds the document at most every 0.4 s for all viewers, and a poll with since carries only the new series samples (about 25 KB a poll with 30 streams, under 2 ms to build).

The page has the aggregate decode rate now and its last five minutes stacked by backend, the requests by state (waiting, prefilling, thinking, tool call, writing), TTFT p50 and p90, the cache hit and the cost per minute over the requests finished in the last five minutes; one card per backend; and one lane per request: backend and model, client and session (x-session-id), state, tokens (thinking apart), decode tok/s now and on average, TTFT, prefill rate, cache, cost so far, elapsed. A lane keeps its row until a few seconds after it ends; a new request takes the first free row.

Live token counts, and where each comes from:

backend live count the engine's own requests the engine's count, prefill progress and rate, the state a TandemLLM backend behind the proxy the same: the relay sends X-Tandem-Relay-Id, the engine files the request under it, and the proxy reads the engine's /v1/dashboard/parallel once a second while it has requests there (it answers a trusted local caller or the admin token). The engine streams blocks of several tokens, so its frames are not a count any other backend its stream frames, only after they were checked: each finished streamed answer's frames are compared with its usage.completion_tokens (within 2 tokens and 1 %), answers with text only and answers with tool calls apart. Two passing answers of a kind and no failing one among its last 8 make those frames a count. DeepSeek's reasoning and content frames are one token each; its tool-call arguments arrive several tokens a frame, so a DeepSeek lane has no live count while it writes a call

Without a count a lane shows its frames and "not reported"; its tokens and rate come with the usage at the end. A relayed request's prompt and cached tokens arrive with the usage too ("at the end"). Cost so far is the completion tokens so far at the output price, marked + until the usage adds the prompt's part.

tools/parallel_load.py drives the page: N agent-like sessions (a system prompt, two tools, up to three streamed turns each, tool results fed back) over the models you name, for example --mix deepseek-flash=10,fake-a=18,TandemLLM=2 --duration 90 --budget-usd 0.5 --board. It reports TTFT, decode rate, cache hit, throughput and cost per model, stops starting turns at the budget, and with --board puts the page's per-second series beside the frames its own clients received.

docs.title: Prices and cost
docs.text:
A streamed request with X-Tandem-Cost: 1 (the Chat tab's chatd sends it) gets the request's cost as one SSE comment just before data: [DONE]: : tandem-cost {"cost_micros": 6140, "backend": "deepseek"}, every request the harness sent for it summed, the figure its ledger row gets; cost_micros is null without a price. SSE readers skip comments; without the header the stream is the backend's, byte for byte.

A price row per model holds USD per million tokens for input, cached input, cache write and output, and optionally cache_write_1h, the price of a cache write kept for 1 hour (the cache write price without one; TANDEM_PRICE_<n> takes it as a fifth value). The cost of a request is (prompt - cached - cache write) x input + cached x cached input + cache write x its price (1-hour writes at theirs) + completion x output, written into the row when the request ends, so a later price change never rewrites history. A model without a price has a null cost. DeepSeek charges half outside its peak hours (01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC on weekdays); a price row can carry an offpeak block, and the DeepSeek adapter picks by the request's UTC hour. Chinese public holidays count as peak here, so their cost reads high.

The proxy never fetches a price list. proxy/prices.seed.json holds the list prices of OpenAI and DeepSeek as read from their pages on 2026-10-04; the model rows offer them and apply them only on a click. Check the providers' pages before you bill anyone from these numbers.

docs.title: Users and their keys
docs.text: People sign in with accounts; programs use API tokens, made per person or tool on the Access page and shown once (auth.md). Another device needs a token with the protocol's scope and the protocol's exposure on network. The token's owner goes into the ledger's user column.

docs.title: Who may change the configuration
docs.text: Reading /v1/config needs a signed-in account or a token with settings:read; a write needs an operator's session or a token with settings:write (auth.md). Being on the same machine opens nothing outside local mode. The default bind is 127.0.0.1; the page is meant for a trusted network. Never put it on the internet.

docs.title: Terms, in short
docs.text: Using your own key through your own proxy for your own clients is ordinary API use. Putting one key in front of several people makes you the provider toward them: the provider's terms hold the key holder responsible for what those people send, and most forbid reselling access without an agreement. Per-user keys keep each person's usage visible in the ledger. This is not legal advice.

docs.title: The harness in front of a backend
docs.text:
The conductor runs in front of other backends too: the router's task class, the effort, the packages and skills as notes, the side requests' caps, the session's memory and its /s/<token> address, the library and Laya, the loop guards, E1 and the tool checks, the compaction section and the state lines. In the engine's server it is the engine's own conductor (--backends with --conductor-config); the standalone proxy keeps one of its own under --conductor-config (default ~/.tandemllm/conductor, off for none), with its journal in the usage ledger's file as on the engine. A backend's harness.mode turns it on: off (the default) is the relay above, byte for byte; shadow journals what it would do and changes nothing; on acts. harness.profile picks the conductor profile for that backend's requests (empty: by client, as on the engine). Both are on the backend's form and in TANDEM_BACKEND_<ID>_HARNESS and _HARNESS_PROFILE.

Per model, each feature group can be inherit, off, shadow or on, and the model can override the mode. A group is never above the mode. What inherit means:

group what it does over HTTP local engines cloud APIs class the router's question asked of the backend itself, with its own constraint field (vLLM structured_outputs.choice, SGLang regex, OpenAI a JSON-schema enum, plain text otherwise) on on effort the backend's own switch: chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking, reasoning_effort (OpenAI's o-series and gpt-5 only), thinking.type (DeepSeek); a budget is a word, never a cap on on packages the router's note at the end of the newest user message, replayed on later turns at the same message index on off side a client's title or summary call capped (64 or 256 tokens) with thinking off on on loops D1 and D2 on the streamed words; the tool-argument guard on the streamed arguments on on e1 an empty answer to a request with tools gets a second request with a hidden user turn on off tools C1 to C4 on the answer's calls; a regenerate is a second request on shadow compaction the TandemLLM section appended to a compaction request on on states the state lines in the stream on on memory the memory card and notes at the end of the user message, the model's blocks taken out of the stream and written; the background writer as one more request in the backend's idle time (TANDEM_BACKEND_<ID>_WRITER: auto is off on a paid model; a daily spend and run cap; docs/memory.md) on shadow

The Backends screen shows, next to each switch, what it resolves to, one sentence on what it costs or loses on that backend, and what its extra requests cost over the last 24 hours (the class questions are ledger rows of the client harness; a second request's tokens and cost are in its journal row). The Compare view lists shadow precision per backend.

docs.title: What is different from the engine
docs.text:
The note is text at the end of the user's message, inside the <runtime-note> frame the router uses, not ids before the end of the turn, so a model can quote it. The replay keeps the bytes of the conversation's head the same from turn to turn, so a backend with a prefix cache (vLLM, SGLang, OpenAI's and DeepSeek's prompt caches) keeps its match: the hash covers each message's role, content, name and tool calls up to the noted one. A client that rewrites its history breaks the hash; the note is gone and the router adds its block again, as on the engine.

The class question is a request of its own, a few hundred prompt tokens each. A new user message can ask up to three (the class, the package among several candidates, a library skill); a tool turn and a repeated message ask none. On the engine the same questions cost nothing beside the turn. With the harness on, proxy_ms includes the time the plan took, the questions included.

E1, the regenerate and the reasoning close are second requests. The client gets one stream: the second answer goes out as the continuation of the first, with the first chunk's id, no second role delta and one [DONE]. To make that possible the proxy holds the finish frame, the usage frame and [DONE] until the turn is settled, and holds the tool-call frames while a check can act. When the client asked for usage, the usage frame it gets is the sum of every request, and so is the ledger row. A reasoning close needs continue_final_message (the vllm and sglang kinds); on any other backend D1 and D2 are journaled in shadow with no_continue_final_message. A request that is not streamed gets the plan (the note, the effort, the side cap, the compaction section) but none of the monitor's acts, which read the stream.

docs.title: The word-level loop detector
docs.text: D1's three arms (a repeated pattern, the repeat share of the history, the novelty of the last window) run over words instead of tokens (tandemapp/conductor/monitor/tier0_words.py), with numbers measured for words, never the token ones copied. tools/loop_words_fp.py streams the opencode database's reasoning through it. On 2026-10-04: 2,674 finished turns whose reasoning compresses under 5 times, and 20 loops (turns the token limit cut inside the reasoning, or reasoning that compresses 8 times or more). The strictest of 32 settings fires on 6 of the finished turns and catches 11 of the 20 loops. The engine's own D1 acted on that traffic, so some of those 6 may be loops it closed; the text alone does not say which. The shipped words block in ops/supervisor.yaml therefore says calibrated: false, and every D1 verdict over the proxy stays in shadow until the Compare view's labels show its precision.

docs.title: Laya, the library and the session address
docs.text: The standalone proxy serves GET /v1/library[/...], and POST /v1/laya/ask when the conductor's decider role names a Jev endpoint over HTTP. Both also answer under /s/<token>/, the address the notes give the model, and are journaled to that session. The classifier role may name a backend (backend:<id>/<model>) to answer the class question instead of the request's own backend, and the narrator role the same for the state lines, inside its latency budget; without one the lines are the templates.

docs.title: License
docs.text: The proxy, the collector and the package are part of TandemLLM and carry its licenses: AGPL-3.0-only, or the commercial license in COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md. Under the AGPL, anyone who runs a changed copy of the dashboard as a service for others must offer those users the changed source. The one runtime dependency, cryptography, is Apache-2.0 or BSD at the user's choice; the host extra adds psutil (BSD-3-Clause) and nvidia-ml-py (BSD-3-Clause). NOTICE lists them. None of their code is copied into this repository. The two plugins in plugins/ are part of TandemLLM too, under the same license, and have no dependencies; vLLM and SGLang (Apache-2.0) are the engines they run in, not part of them.

docs.title: Not in this release
docs.text: A release on PyPI (the wheel builds; publishing it is a separate step). The cloud adapters and the harness's second requests are tested against the providers' documented shapes and a fake backend, not against a paid call or a real vLLM or SGLang; tools/proxy_harness_check.py runs the harness in front of a live TandemLLM engine. The per-process GPU memory on a discrete GPU is tested against a recorded NVML answer, not yet on such a machine. The vLLM and SGLang tables are tested on pages built from each release's own metric definitions, and the plugins on stand-ins built from each release's own classes; tools/proxy_engines_check.sh --plugins checks both against running servers.

docs.title: The session monitor
docs.text: The session monitor is the conductor's second half. The router plans a turn before it runs; the monitor watches the turn while it runs and acts when the model goes wrong in a way it can recognise without guessing: a reasoning block that goes in circles, an answer that ends empty, a tool call that does not parse, the same call a third time, a claim of done without the evidence. This page lists where it may act, what it may do, and each task.

docs.title: Modes and policy
docs.text:
--conductor raw|shadow|on switches it. raw, the code default, runs none of it, and nothing closes a reasoning block but a budget. shadow runs every rule and journals what it would do, and executes nothing. on, the shipped profile's value, executes each task in the mode its policy gives it. A request's X-Tandem header can lower the mode, never raise it, and a request with n above 1 never acts.

The policy is a file, ops/supervisor.yaml, validated at start against ops/supervisor.schema.json. It holds every task's mode (off, shadow, act), every threshold and every text the monitor may write. The conductor keeps it as its monitor document, versioned and edited like the others, and a profile's tasks section overrides a task's mode per profile.

docs.title: Safe points and actions
docs.text:
The monitor acts only at four safe points, from a fixed set of actions.

flowchart LR
    sp4(["SP4 before the prefill<br/>note, think budget"]) --> pre[prefill]
    pre --> blk["reasoning: verify blocks"]
    blk -- "SP1 after each block<br/>close the reasoning, give up" --> blk
    blk --> ans[answer]
    ans --> sp2(["SP2 at the end token<br/>continue hidden, give up"])
    sp2 --> sp3(["SP3 the held tool calls<br/>repair, regenerate, give up"])

The session monitor's four safe points on one request: before the prefill, after each committed block, at the end token before it reaches the client, and when the answer's held tool calls are complete.

point when actions SP4 the prompt is rendered, before the prefill PROMPT_TAIL_NOTE, SET_THINK_BUDGET SP1 a verify block is committed CLOSE_REASONING, GIVE_UP SP2 the model wrote its end token, before the client sees it CONTINUE_HIDDEN, GIVE_UP SP3 the answer ended and its tool calls are held REPAIR_CALL, REGENERATE_CALL, GIVE_UP

Safe points and the actions each allows.

What the client sees is little. A hidden close forwards the policy's phrase through the engine and streams only from the closer on (</think> in the tags format). A hidden continue drops the end token and forwards a nudge, and the answer follows in the same response. GIVE_UP is one visible sentence with finish stop. Hidden tokens are never in usage, never in the suffix store, and a response the monitor acted on is not stored in the response cache. The KV holds them, and the end anchor puts them back into the next prompt where the rows hold them (TandemEngine's caches).

Caps hold the monitor back: at most 2 acts a request and 6 a session hour in the shipped policy, and never the same hidden action twice in a row on one turn. Beyond a cap a decision is journaled and not executed.

docs.title: The tasks
docs.text:
task rule what it catches, and what it does mode D1 reasoning_loop a reasoning block that goes in circles (below); closes it, hidden act D2 reasoning_backstop reasoning that reaches 32,768 tokens, or the output limit less 2,048; closes it act E1 empty_turn an end token inside the reasoning, or an empty answer to a request that offered tools; tool calls the model wrote inside its reasoning go out as its answer when they parse and name an offered tool, else continues hidden, then gives up after two tries act E2 claim_check a coding turn that ends claiming the work is done without the tool evidence (below); acts in the coding, hermes and chat-app profiles, shadow in overnight act C4 malformed_call a tool-call block that does not parse; repairs it when the fix is not a guess, else has the model write it again act C3 repeated_call the same call a third time after identical results; asks for something different act C5 sequential_mutations an answer with two or more calls that change something outside the conversation (send, schedule, create, write, delete, read off each tool's declaration); has the model write them again one at a time, each after the last one's result shadow; act in tools C1 risk_floor rm -rf outside the project root, git push, a write outside the root, a download piped into a shell shadow C2 project_rules what text alone can decide of the project's AGENTS.md: a numbered copy of a file, a path under /tmp/, a written file over 400 lines shadow S1 gate_stagnation a checker gate that failed 3 times in a row without getting closer; one hidden note act S2 context_health after a compaction, two tool steps that read none of the state files; one hidden note act S4 stall_watchdog no file changed, nothing committed and no checker number better for 20 minutes; one hidden note, and a push when the client has gone act S5 turn_budget on every client: the same problem stated three times; a build turn three minutes and five tool steps in with nothing written; an Open WebUI turn past 12 minutes without a new product file, or 18 in any case; one hidden note act

The session monitor's tasks, with their shipped modes.

Each profile sets its tasks' modes on top of the policy. S5 runs under every profile that runs the monitor and needs no state file. The session tasks S1, S2 and S4 act only in the overnight profile, and only in a project whose system prompt names a PROGRESS.yaml; the tool checks run where the profile holds calls (the coding and overnight profiles).

docs.title: Reasoning loops
docs.text: D1 watches the reasoning with three arms: a pattern of 1 to 16 tokens repeated at least 4 times over 128 tokens or more; the share of the last 256 tokens' 16-grams already seen earlier in the block, checked every 64 tokens once the block has 2,048; and novelty collapse, the share of new 8-grams in the last 128 tokens falling under 0.1. When an arm fires in act mode, the monitor closes the block with a hidden phrase and the model answers from what it has. D2 is the backstop: no reasoning block runs past 32,768 tokens, or past the output limit less 2,048, so an answer always has room. With the conductor raw, nothing closes a block but a budget.

docs.title: Tool-call checks
docs.text:
With a tool-call task able to act, every call of an answer is held until the answer ends; a block that does not parse is held too, not let out as content. At the end token every call is checked by every SP3 task before any is released. If all pass, the calls go out whole, each in one delta with an id made at release. If any act fails, none goes out: the end token is dropped, a hidden turn shaped as the calls' tool result carries the reminders, and the model writes the set again in the same response. An answer that ended without its end token (the token limit) cannot be written again, so there a failure gives up. A block the client's own stop string cut is let out as the text it was.

C4's repairs are deterministic: JSON with trailing commas or Python literals, an unquoted name, a closing tag that never came. It checks arguments against the tool's JSON schema (required keys, types) in shadow. The tool-argument loop guard (TandemEngine's server) runs beside these checks and also stops a call that streams live.

docs.title: The claim check: E2
docs.text: A model can end a coding turn with “done, verified in the browser” after a test that set a key's state in code instead of pressing it, or that read a lost game as a working one. E2 checks such a claim before the end token reaches the client. The trigger is structural: the turn's class is one of the building classes, the request offered tools, and the model wrote its end token after a non-empty answer with no tool call. Then Qwen itself answers, thinking off, one letter a question: does the message tell the user the work is done; and if so, what the tool evidence since the last write says (supported, no run after the last write, errors in the evidence, an unexplained surprise, a faked test). The questions are asked in place, inside the conversation the engine holds, because a request to the server's own port would wait for the lock the turn holds. In act mode an unsupported claim gets a hidden note with the turn's evidence digest, and the model continues.

docs.title: Turn snapshots and outcomes
docs.text:
A profile's outcomes section drives a structural reading of each tool-result turn, every switch off when absent.

  • The snapshot: from the request body alone, what the session did since the last one: the calls, the files written, each screenshot's hash and size, a console's level counts and error lines, checker lines, exit codes, a test runner's counts, a state dump's diff. It is stored beside the transcript block, at most 32 KB, and takes about 0.023 ms a request (measured).
  • The outcome: the first label whose facts matched, in order: no visible change (the same screenshot after a write), regression, error, low quality, surprise, stuck, tool misuse, a faked test (a script that assigns to a member of an object it did not declare), an environment error, lost context; else progress or none. Every fact is structural; no word decides what anybody meant.
  • In act mode an outcome raises the turn's effort (no visible change and regression to xhigh, error to high) for two tool turns or until progress, and the acting outcomes add their note once per signature.
  • Retrieval: a low-quality or stuck outcome asks the package question over the test skills, and the package that fits becomes the note.

docs.title: Session tasks
docs.text:
Three tasks look across turns. They read what a request carries about the turns before it, each call taken once per session by its id, so a retried request counts nothing twice. Each acts with one hidden note at the end of the prompt, and a request carries at most one of their notes. S1 watches a checker gate (a line such as RESULT: FAIL <- ... from a project's checker) that fails three times in a row without getting closer to its limit. S2 watches the first two tool steps after a compaction for a read of the state files. S4 watches for 20 minutes without a change, a commit or a better number. When no request comes for S4's minutes after a turn ended, the client has gone, and with the policy's notify on the watch sends a push to TANDEM_NOTIFY_URL; the URL is empty in the shipped policy.

S5, the turn budget, watches the turn: the requests that carry the same last user message. Its first arm reads the model's own visible text between its tool calls: when the first sentence states the same problem three times among the last eight problem sentences (shared word triples, a number in common), the note tells it to stop tuning, deliver what works and say what is untested. An Open WebUI agent chat had a working game after 25 minutes and then wrote “The bot is stuck at x=436” seven times while it tuned its own playtest bot; it never answered. The second arm watches a build turn: three minutes and five tool steps in, with nothing the user asked for written (a write outside the scratch directory, /tmp, logs and pid files), the note says to write the deliverable first. The third is a wall clock for a chat client someone waits in front of (Open WebUI): after 12 minutes of tool calls with no product file in the last 4, or after 18 in any case, the note says to finish and answer, and every 4 minutes after it a shorter one. Replayed on that chat, the notes come at 3.1, 18.0 and 36.0 minutes; on four clean opencode runs it adds none (measured). The fourth arm, verify, watches what follows the deliverable: when the steps since the last product write wrote only scratch files, two of them test tools (scripts or pages, not logs or data), and 90 s have passed since that write, the note says to stop building test tools, check once with a tool that works here and answer. An opencode page run wrote its page at 176 s, its last product edit at 257 s, then spent the run's remaining five minutes on a browser driver of its own; replayed, the note comes at 347 s, and four clean opencode runs get none (measured). Time alone is not a reason: opencode has no clock, and a chat client has the wall clock's quiet rule. A box whose policy is a stored document gets S5, or the keys its stored S5 lacks, with tools/monitor_migrate.py.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Every decision, passes included, is one journal row and one [conductor] log line with the task, the decision, the reason and counts, never a text. The ledger's requests row gets conductor_acts, conductor_hidden_tokens and conductor_acted, and the dashboard's speed figures leave out the requests the conductor acted in. Prometheus counts every decision and action (qse_conductor_*). GET /v1/conductor/events lists the decisions, and GET /v1/conductor/watch what the session tasks hold per session.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text: The interface the policy engine builds on is kept stable. A rule is tier0.register(name, safe_point, params, required, doc) on a function from an event to an action; params is the JSON Schema of the task's parameters, which the policy schema picks up. The events are RequestEvent, BlockEvent, FinishEvent and ToolCallEvent. An action is one of the fixed set. python tools/conductor_policy.py --schema writes the schema from the rule registry, and python tools/conductor_policy.py <file> checks a policy file.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
TandemApp keeps its settings where they always were: the page's switches and the backends in the controller's config database, the conductor's documents in their folder, each engine's settings on its own host. /v1/settings is one interface over all of them. Every part of it answers the same six questions, a change can span several parts, and every change is versioned, can be undone and is audited.

The contract is contracts/settings-v1.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
scope target store restart class app controller the page's switches: chat and conductor, on or off none backends controller the config database: backends.<id>.<field>, backends.<id>.key, routes, users.<id>.enabled none conductor controller this controller's conductor documents: settings, router, roles, packages, monitor, residency, deciders, profiles.<name> hot engine an engine host's id the engine's managed overlay, through tandem remote settings over SSH per key: hot or engine hooks controller the hook registry and the decision providers, through their adapter: hooks.<id>.<field>, providers.<id>.<field> none; an in-process hook needs an engine restart plugins an installed plugin's id the plugin registry: enabled, settings.<property>, secrets.<NAME>, capabilities.<capability>, trust (plugins) none

They apply in this order. A change to the backends lands before a conductor document that may name one, and both land before an engine restart. Hooks apply before plugins, so a change set that turns off a plugin and the hooks that name it lets go of the hooks first.

The restart classes:

  • none: the change applies as it is.
  • app: this controller restarts.
  • hot: the running service reads the change at once.
  • engine: the engine restarts. This is scheduled and waits for the engine to be idle.

An engine reached over HTTP only, a TandemLLM backend whose host is not paired over SSH, is a read-only target, http:<backend id>. Its hot keys are read from the engine's GET /v1/engine/settings. To change it, use its own host (tandem remote settings), or pair it.

docs.title: The six operations
docs.text:
Every scope answers:

GET  /v1/settings/{scope}/schema[?target=]      each key: type, default, restart class, fingerprint flag, secret, writable
GET  /v1/settings/{scope}[?target=]             each key's value and where it comes from
POST /v1/settings/{scope}/plan     {target?, set?, unset?}
POST /v1/settings/{scope}/apply    {target?, set?, unset?, confirm, confirm_fingerprint?, confirm_grant?, when?, deadline_s?, note?}
GET  /v1/settings/{scope}/versions[?target=]
POST /v1/settings/{scope}/restore  {target?, version, confirm?, ...}     without confirm: the plan

GET /v1/settings lists the scopes in order with their targets.

  • Sources. In app, a source is install while the env file decides (TANDEM_CHAT, TANDEM_CONDUCTOR) and page once switched. Unsetting a key hands it back to the install. In backends, a field the environment sets is env and not writable here. Its variable names the variable to change instead. Engine keys carry the engine's own layer names (default, install, profile, setup, local, managed, mode).
  • Versions. The conductor and the engine have versions of their own: <document>@<n> and the overlay's n. For app, backends and hooks, the controller keeps the values after each change in its config database. Secrets are left out. A change made on another screen is recorded as a version of its own ("as found") before the next change.
  • Restore writes a new version equal to the old one. It never deletes history. A key that no longer exists, or that the environment now sets, is left alone and the plan says so. A conductor document or an engine overlay that is no longer valid is refused with restore_invalid.

docs.title: Change sets
docs.text:
POST /v1/settings/plan  {changes: [{scope, target?, set?, unset?}, {scope, target?, restore: "<version>"}, ...]}
POST /v1/settings/apply {changes, confirm, confirm_fingerprint?, confirm_grant?, when?, deadline_s?, note?}

A change set has at most one part per scope and target.

Unsetting a key that is unset already is no change, in every scope: the plan drops it, and a part left with nothing applies as unchanged. In backends, a field that holds nothing is unset (set false).

The plan writes nothing. For each part it lists:

  • every change, with its restart class;
  • for a part that restarts an engine, how long the restart itself takes (restart_estimate, below);
  • the keys that feed an engine's disk-cache fingerprint;
  • warnings.

restart_estimate is {seconds, source}. The source is one of these, in this order:

source seconds measured what this controller saw the last time it restarted that engine: from the engine's job acting to the end of the warm-up. Kept while the controller runs. engine the engine's last start as its status reports it: its last start, restart or settings job that acted at once, from its creation to its end default 180

It leaves out the wait for idle, which deadline_s bounds.

It gives one confirm for the whole set. A key that feeds the fingerprint adds confirm_fingerprint: after that restart every saved prefix and parked chat misses, so it asks twice.

A refusal while a part is planned names the part: its scope and target, and the key when it is about one key's value (unknown_key, locked, bad_value, invalid_document, extension_missing). The same key on two engine hosts is told apart. A part of one key names that key even when its store's sentence does not.

Applying plans again and compares:

situation answer no confirm 428 confirm_required the settings changed since the plan 409 stale_plan, with the new plan a fingerprint key without its second confirm 428 fingerprint_confirm_required another change set is applying 409 busy

The parts then apply in order. The first failure stops the set. The answer lists each part:

state meaning applied written scheduled an engine restart will run it (see below) unchanged it held already failed refused or failed; error says why not_run after the failure, untouched

Each applied part carries the version it had before and the restore that brings it back. The set as a whole is applied, partial, failed or unchanged.

Applying again. The same confirm with the same body, sent again within five minutes, answers the same result (replayed true). Nothing is applied twice. After a partial failure, plan the same changes again: the parts that already hold are unchanged, and the rest is planned anew.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A backend's API key, and any key a hook adapter marks secret, is write-only:

  • an answer shows set true or false, never the value;
  • a plan shows the change as set or unset;
  • the confirm binds the value through its hash only.

No answer, version, audit row, log line or export holds a secret. A restore leaves secrets as they are.

The engine's keys that may hold a secret are not managed by its overlay. Their values are not read into an answer either.

docs.title: Engine changes and restarts
docs.text:
Hot changes. A change of hot keys only (today QSE_ALLOW_FROM) goes through the engine's PATCH /v1/engine/settings (engine API 1.9). The plan's overlay version is the base. There is no restart.

Other changes go through tandem remote settings apply. when sets when the engine acts, deadline_s how long it waits:

  • when: idle (the default) waits for idle, up to deadline_s (600 s by default);
  • when: now acts at once;
  • when: at=<ISO time> waits until that time, then for idle.

The engine's own job stops the engine, makes the new overlay version current and starts it. If the start fails, the engine puts the last good version back.

The restart. The controller follows the engine's job (GET /v1/settings/restarts/{id}, in the part's restart):

state what happens scheduled waiting for an at= time. Nothing is drained yet. draining the gateway answers 503 node_draining with Retry-After: 30 for the backends on that engine host. Other backends keep serving. The engine's job waits for idle. remaining_s counts down to the deadline. restarting the job acts: stop, new version, start. warming the job is done. One token goes through each backend on the host, then the backends serve again. done, failed, timeout, cancelled the end.
  • failed: the engine's message, and restored, the version it runs again and whether it answers.
  • timeout: the deadline passed while the engine was busy. It changed nothing.
  • cancelled: see below.

Cancel. POST /v1/settings/restarts/{id}/cancel works while the restart is scheduled or draining. The controller sends start to the engine host. That replaces a job that still waits, and finds the engine healthy, so nothing changes. Once the job acts it is too late (409 too_late).

The drains live in the controller's process. A controller restart ends them; the engine's job goes on by itself.

docs.title: The engine's mode
docs.text:
Two keys of the engine scope stand for the engine's mode:

key values what it is mode engine or chat engine: the bare engine. chat: TandemApp's conductor and Chat run inside it. mode.ext a module, tandemapp.engine_ext by default the extension chat mode runs

They show what the engine's QSE_MODE and QSE_EXT resolve to. Those two are not changed directly: a part that names them is refused (422 locked).

  • The mode alone. A part that only sets mode and mode.ext goes through the engine's own tandem remote mode set. It plans, applies and restarts like any other engine change: the change set's id, the audit rows, when and deadline_s, the drain, the countdown, Cancel and the warm-up token. The restart's kind is mode.
  • With other keys. Together with other keys of the same engine, the mode goes into the same overlay change as QSE_MODE and QSE_EXT, which is what mode set writes. The engine restarts once.
  • The extension. When the result is chat mode, the plan asks the engine host for its extensions (tandem remote ext list). If none of that module loads there, the plan says so in a warning and names the wheel TandemApp installs first: its own, for its own version (TANDEM_NODE_WHEEL, else built from this controller's copy, as Add Spark sends it). The apply sends it (tandem remote ext install, its sha256 checked) before the switch. The install itself restarts nothing.
  • No wheel. A module that is not TandemApp's, or no wheel on this controller, makes the plan refuse with 409 extension_missing on the key mode.ext. The sentence says what to do: set TANDEM_NODE_WHEEL to the tandemapp wheel of this release, or install the extension on the engine host.

POST /v1/fleet/engines/{id}/mode {mode?, when?, ext?}, the route the Add engine wizard uses, is a change set of one part with these keys. It answers as before: whether anything changed, the mode before and the engine's job. Its audit row names the change set.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
GET /v1/settings/audit[?change_set=cs-...] lists the settings' rows of the config database's audit table, which /v1/config/audit shows too:

  • one row per part applied or restored (settings.apply, settings.restore) with its result;
  • one row per change set (settings.change_set) with what applied, what failed and what did not run;
  • one row per restart's end (settings.restart) and per cancel (settings.cancel).

Each row has the change set's id, the scope and target, the keys (never a value), who, when and the result. Every row a store writes during a change set carries the same id, for example a backend's update or a switch of the page.

docs.title: Rights
docs.text:
request rule reads the dashboard's plans, applies, restores, a cancel the configuration's: the admin from another machine, or a tool on this machine

Every write must come from the page itself: a JSON body, not from another site or origin.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
The hooks scope is an adapter (settingscopes.HooksAdapter). The controller plugs in the hook registry's (proxy/hooksettings.py). Without one, the scope answers an empty schema.

Each hook has these keys:

key what hooks.<id>.enabled whether it is called at all hooks.<id>.mode off, shadow or on hooks.<id>.priority its order among the hooks of a stage, low first hooks.<id>.scope the requests it runs on: lists of patterns under models, backends, profiles, users, sessions, client_kinds. Unset: every request. hooks.<id>.policy open or closed when it fails. Unset: the stage's default. hooks.<id>.timeout_ms its own time limit. Unset: the stage's budget. hooks.<id>.payload meta, redacted or full hooks.<id>.secret an http hook's signing secret, shown only as set or unset

Each value carries the hook's name as its label. The checks are the registry's own. A change is written through the registry and audited there, and the hook runner reads it at the next request. The settings interface keeps a version after each change.

Adding or removing a hook, where and when it runs, and a new secret stay on the hooks' API (/v1/fleet/hooks, hooks). That API makes the secret and shows it once, so the settings interface never writes one.

docs.title: The full payload
docs.text:
Setting payload to full grants the hook the prompts and answers as they are. It keeps the rules of the hooks' API:

  • Only a caller with pairing's rights may plan it: the admin, or this machine while no admin password is set. Anyone else gets 403 trust_required.
  • The plan warns with the destination's host.
  • A destination outside the LAN needs a second confirm. The plan lists the key under grant_keys and gives confirm_grant. Apply without it is 428 grant_confirm_required. The grant records who confirmed it.

docs.title: Decision providers
docs.text:
The decision providers are keys of the same scope. They sit beside the hooks because a hook provider is a decision.ask hook. Each provider has these keys:

key what providers.<id>.enabled whether it is asked at all providers.<id>.mode on, shadow or ab providers.<id>.ab_percent in ab, the share it answers, 0 to 100 providers.<id>.sticky in ab, what the share sticks to: session, user or request providers.<id>.questions the questions it answers, each {model?, endpoint?, timeout_ms?} providers.<id>.api_key a systemone-http provider's own key providers.<id>.questions.<question>.api_key the key for one question alone; a change set that adds the question to questions may set it in the same change

A key is write-only. A string sets it and an unset clears it. An answer says only whether one is set, with its hint, and a version never holds it. A question's key exists once the provider answers that question: add the question first, then its key.

One enabled provider serves a question on or ab. A change set may move a question from one provider to another. The provider that lets it go is written first.

Adding or removing a provider and its kind stay on its API (/v1/fleet/decision-providers, decision providers).

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
The plugins scope (settings-v1 1.1) has one target a plugin. Its keys come from the plugin's manifest, so they differ plugin by plugin; each plugin keeps its own versions, and restoring one never touches another or the hooks. Installing, upgrading and removing a plugin stay on its API (/v1/fleet/plugins, plugins).

key what enabled the plugin host may start it. The tree is checked against its recorded sha256 first. settings.<property> one property of the plugin's settings schema, with its type and default. A value must hold against the property's schema. Unset: the default. secrets.<NAME> a declared secret, write-only, sealed under the master key capabilities.<capability> a requested capability, false until granted. Unset revokes it. trust only for a plugin whose manifest asks trust: host: host lets it run as a process of the app's user, outside any sandbox; sandboxed (the default) keeps it from starting. Set to host here only for a plugin signed by a key trusted for host; an unsigned plugin's grant takes the typed confirmation on its trust route (plugins), and here answers 409.

Enabling a plugin and every grant take pairing's rights (403 trust_required otherwise). A grant of prompts:full, engine:control, network:<host> outside the LAN or trust host is in the plan's grant_keys and needs confirm_grant. The plugin host restarts a running plugin when its settings, secrets or grants change. A restore that brings a grant back asks again.

docs.title: The configuration as a file
docs.text:
GET /v1/fleet/app/export writes the configuration as a file (tandemapp-fleet-config, version 2): the fleet's nodes, deployments, alert rules, layouts and app.* settings, and the hooks, the decision providers, the plugins (name, version, source, sha256, settings and grants, never their files), each paired engine host's overlay and the conductor's stored documents. No secret is in it: a hook's secret, a provider's keys, a plugin's secrets and an engine's secret keys appear by name only.

POST /v1/fleet/app/import {config, mode?} plans the file and changes nothing; POST /v1/fleet/app/import/apply with the plan's confirm applies it. Version 2's switches, settings, grants, overlay keys and documents go through one change set of this interface, in its order, stopping at the first failure; the hooks and providers the file adds are created after it, the hooks first. A plugin the file names that is not installed is a conflict naming what to install, and so is a hook of that plugin; an engine host that is not paired is a conflict. A plan whose change set feeds an engine's disk-cache fingerprint, or that grants a payload outside the LAN, gives confirm_fingerprint or confirm_grant, and the apply sends them too. A secret the file holds by mistake is stripped and listed in the plan's stripped. A version 1 file still imports; a file of a later version is refused with the version it needs.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
The dashboard shows this interface under Settings, App: one page per scope.

page what it holds App the app scope: the Chat and conductor switches under What runs here, above the controller's own page Backends the backends scope: a group for each backend, the routing rules, the users' keys Conductor the conductor scope: each document, edited whole Engines the engine scope: a page for each engine host, its mode first (the two choice cards, and the extension once chat is chosen). An HTTP-only one is read-only and says why. Hooks the hooks pages (hooks) and the decision providers' (decision providers). They stage their switches as keys of the hooks scope. Under the pipeline the same keys show as a plain form, a group for each hook and each provider. Plugins the plugins pages (plugins). A plugin's switch, settings, secrets, grants and trust level are staged as keys of the plugins scope, one target a plugin. Under a plugin's page the same keys show as a plain form, with the plugin's own versions. History the audit rows and the restarts that ended. #/app/history?change_set=cs-... shows one change set.

Each page draws its form from the scope's schema. A key gets the control its type asks for: a switch for on and off, a number field for an integer, a JSON editor for a document. The row also shows the default and the value's source. The environment locks some keys; such a row names the variable, for example TANDEM_BACKENDS. No page shows a secret. You set one or remove it.

Changing a field writes nothing. The page stages the change, and a bar at the bottom carries the staged changes from page to page. Review then reads the plan of the whole set from POST /v1/settings/plan:

  • every part in the order it applies, with its changes and warnings;
  • whether a part restarts an engine, and how long the restart takes ("about 3 min"). The plan then asks when: once idle (it waits 10 minutes by default), at a set time, or now;
  • a second confirm for a key that feeds the fingerprint, and for a hook's full payload outside the LAN. That one names the hooks and where their payload goes.

A plan the controller refuses for one field marks that field, on the page of the part the refusal names, with the sentence under it.

Apply answers with each part's state. An applied part has a Restore button. After a failure you can plan the same changes again.

While an engine restarts, every page of the area shows it: the state, the countdown to the deadline, the engine's job, and Cancel while can_cancel holds. After a failed start the card names the version the engine runs again.

Versions sit at the bottom of each page, with what differs from now. A restore goes through the same plan as any other change.

docs.title: Status lines, the voice and the shadow reader
docs.text: A client shows the model's reasoning and its answer. What the conductor does around them, the engine's queue, a long prefill, a hidden close, was visible only on the dashboard. This page covers the lines that show it in the client, the small model that can write them, and a second use of small models: the shadow reader that keeps its own exact copy of a session.

docs.title: Status lines
docs.text:
With a profile's ui.states: on (the shipped profiles), each step the conductor takes is one short line the client renders, at the moment it happens:

› code edit, maximum effort
› reading 20,745 tokens, about 18 s left
› waiting: another request is running, position 1, about 40 s
› thinking 25 s: designing a 140x15 tile map with pits, coins, enemies and platforms
› writing render.js, 211 lines so far
› checking the tool call
kind template when route deciding: code_edit, high effort a classifier answered this turn package retrieving: skill photo-to-3d the note carries a skill cap thinking closed at the 16,384 cap the turn's cap closes the reasoning backstop thinking closed at the 32,768 backstop D2 closes it loop loop detected, steering D1 closes a reasoning loop continue empty answer, continuing E1's hidden continue check checking the tool call SP3 checks the held calls repair repairing the tool call C4 repairs a call queue waiting: ..., position 1 the request waits for the engine prefill reading 35,189 tokens at ~750 tok/s, about 47 s left a long prefill, every 10 s thinking thinking 4 min, 9,800 tokens every 2 minutes or 4,096 tokens of thinking

Kinds of status line.

ui.states_channel says where the lines go. reasoning puts them inside the reasoning the client renders. content sends each as a content delta of its own, before, between and after the reasoning's parts. inline, the coding profile's value, is built for opencode: each line opens a reasoning part of its own, titled by the line, in time order, and the answer's text part opens after them. It works because opencode's provider ends an open reasoning part when an empty tool_calls delta arrives and opens a new one at the next reasoning delta, which the server sends as **› line**. That was checked by running recorded streams through opencode's own parser, taken out of its binary.

The model never reads a line. Every line is framed so that the server can find it exactly, and whenever the conductor is configured the server takes every framed line out of whatever a client sends back, before the router, the monitor or the template read it. The prompt, the resident prefix it resumes and the notes' replay positions are exactly what they would be without the lines. The lines are not tokens: never in usage, the suffix store or the response cache's key. The journal row keeps each one with its kind and its time.

Open WebUI times a reasoning block from its first reasoning piece to its first answer piece and shows that as “Thought for N seconds”, so the waiting and reading lines counted as thinking: a summary with thinking off that read 12,874 tokens showed “Thought for 14 seconds”. For the client kinds in QWEN38_STATUS_CLIENTS (default open-webui) every line said before the model's first generated token goes out as an Open WebUI status event, the line under the model's name that its tools use, and one last event at the first token says what the wait was (“Read 12,874 tokens in 14 s”). The reasoning opens with the model's own first piece, and a turn that does not think shows no “Thought for”. Lines after the first token keep the profile's channel.

The progress lines (queue, prefill, thinking) are templates with numbers: the queue position and an estimate of the wait, a long prefill's rate and time left, a long thinking's time and tokens (ui.progress). A request that waits for the engine opens its stream at its first waiting line, so a refusal after that ends the stream with an error object and [DONE].

docs.title: The narrator and the voice
docs.text:
ui.narrator picks who writes the lines that are not progress templates.

value lines off the templates on each line rewritten by a small model, in at most 150 ms, else the template thoughts one summary per stretch of thinking of at least 128 tokens: “Thought 1m 43s: planned the level layout and decided on a fixed timestep” live the voice: what the model is doing right now

The narrator's modes.

The voice (live, the coding and chat profiles) separates facts from words. The engine writes the facts: the timer, a tool call's action and target read from the open call block as the model writes it, a write's line count, the queue's place, the prefill's tokens. The small model writes only the short phrase after them, from a window of the model's newest tokens: what the thinking is about now (every 25 s from 15 s), what a thought of at least 10 s decided, what a write is for. Every phrase passes a check before it is said: a file name or number it holds must be in the text the small model read, and so must most of its content words; no first person, no markup, no copy of an example, nothing like the last four lines, and the user's language (English or German). A phrase that fails is not said. Nothing is said for a short turn: no thinking line before 15 s and no tool line for a call done within 1.5 s.

The small model is QWEN38_NARRATOR_MODEL, a Qwen3.5 model (qwen3.5-2b for the voice). It runs on the engine's own Qwen3.5 forward (engine/generative/qwen35.py) and reads the model's own token ids without a second tokenisation, because the Qwen3.5 small models share Qwen3.8's vocabulary and merges; the server checks that at load against the served checkpoint's tokenizer. Its decode step runs from a CUDA graph captured at load, in a memory pool and on a stream of its own. It loads at the start through the residency planner (role narrator, a 6 GiB claim) and stays loaded.

Its time is rationed. The phrases are written in slices of at most 150 ms on the request's own thread, between two of the model's rounds, with the device synchronised first, so nothing of the small model runs beside the big one. A request's small-model time is one share: 3 % of the time since the model's first token (ui.live.share; 2.5 % in the coding profile, which also runs the shadow reader from the same share).

Measured on the engine with Qwen3.5-2B (the 0.4.0 series, the same 2,000-token text and 504 blocks in every run, 3 runs an arm, --no-learn-cost): 63.47 tok/s with the voice off, 62.26 on, -1.90 % (measured).
